subtopic: SUGAR BEETS

speakeroldname: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: SUGAR BEETS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to announce that the agricultural stabilization board has been authorized to support the price of sugar beets for the year 1960 on a national average basis of $14.23 per ton for beets yielding 17 per cent sugar, which is 100 per cent of the 10-year average national price.
For the 1960 crop the stabilization payment will be calculated as the difference between the prescribed price of $14.23 per ton of sugar beets and the average price per ton received by producers in the provinces of Ontario, Manitoba and Alberta. In the case of Quebec, provision has been made for stabilization payments per ton similar to those made in the other three provinces.
In 1958 and 1959 the board supported sugar beets on a regional basis, and the prescribed price for each area was based on the average gross return per pound of sugar in that area. However, with the concurrence of producer organizations in each of the provinces and in line with board policy, the stabilization program for this year will be based on the national average producer return.
Present indications are that there will be a reduced acreage of sugar beets in Ontario this year but an increased acreage in Manitoba and Alberta, and that production may be approximately the same as in 1959.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speechtext:
In
view of the continuing interest and concern of a large number of Canadians in radioactivity, I wish to address a question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare.
Will the minister inform the house whether he has received the report of committee II of the international commission on radiological protection? If so, would he comment on the recommendation it is reported to contain that the maximum permissible levels of strontium 90 found in food and water be lowered from 80 micromicrocuries per litre to 33?
Will the minister also inform the house whether the government intends to give effect to those recommendations?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Monieiih (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: STRONTIUM 90  RECOMMENDATION RESPECTING PERMISSIBLE LEVELS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the hon. member for having given me notice of his intention to ask this question. This department has received the report to which the hon. member refers, and I am pleased to be able to advise him that the substance of its recommendations will be incorporated into the annual report of the radiation protection division for 1959, which will be available later this month.
However, I think it is important to stress that the recommendations made by committee II with respect to maximum permissible concentrations refer to water, but not to food. The maximum permissible concentration in water for strontium 90, applied to the general population, is calculated to be 33 micromicrocuries per litre, assuming a constant intake level for 50 years. On the other hand, based on an average daily intake of approximately 1 gram of calcium, the maximum permissible level

of strontium 90 in the average diet is calculated by my department to be 79 micromicrocuries per gram of calcium.

Mr. Chairman, this is the annual resolution preceding the introduction of the annual bill respecting financing and guarantee of the Canadian National Railways. The legislation follows a form which has been consistently followed since the year 1952.
This year the bill founded upon this resolution will be divided into four major parts, as indicated in the terms of the resolution. The first part authorizes the Canadian National Railways to incur capital expenditures of up to $309,950,000 in the calendar year 1960. The second part authorizes the railway company to make capital expenditures prior to July 1, 1961 to discharge obligations incurred under the act which become due and payable after January 1, 1961 in an amount not exceeding $86 million. The third part authorizes the railway company to enter into contracts for new equipment and for general additions and betterments to the system in an amount not exceeding $51 million. The fourth part provides for the continued purchase by the Minister of Finance of Canadian National Railways 4 per cent preferred stock up to December 31, 1961. This latter provision is new.
Authority provided in the Canadian National Railways Capital Revision Act for the purchase of the railway company's 4 per cent preferred stock to the limit of 3 per cent of the company's gross revenue expires on December 31, 1960. maintopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am sure, as I have always experienced in giving any attention to this legislation, that all members find great difficulty in reconciling any figures that appear at the resolution stage with any prior activities we may have had in the committee to which the minister referred, before which officials of the Canadian National Railways appeared and when there is a discussion in that committee as to their budget for the current year and the capital expenditures that are proposed by the Canadian National Railways. I think those who were members of the sessional committee on railways, air lines and shipping, government owned, will recall that despite what we are reading here, in essence the capital program of the Canadian National Railways, or the borrowing involved in the capital program of the Canadian National Railways for 1960, amounted to the figure of $197.8 million. That was compared with the 1959 bill which was similar to this and which was presented to us at about the same time last year.
That sum of $197.8 million would, we were told, be financed in part by a depreciation availability of $112 million. Some $23 million is provided by reason of the 1951 reorganization legislation under which the government agreed to buy each year 4 per cent preferred stock up to an amount of 3 percent of the revenues of the road. So that actually what is proposed this year is an increase in borrowing of $62.8 million; and we were told in committee by the president that this, when related to the 1959 report, shows a comparable figure of $130.2 million.
Canadian National Railways
Mr. Chairman, I think there is much in the financing of the C.N.R. which gave concern to the members of the committee. In the introductory statement of the president, which will be found on page 23 of the committee report, Mr. Gordon had this rather disappointing summary to make of the railways' affairs. He said that the financial results were most disappointing, particularly in light of the fact that economic activity in 1959 reached new record levels and the gross national product in real terms was approximately 5 per cent greater than in the previous year.
The Minister of Finance will of course recall that we have an argument as to the real value of the growth in the gross national product in 1959. The dominion bureau of statistics has recently calculated that the value of the growth in real terms was 3.5 per cent. None the less, the president reported that notwithstanding this increase in the general economy the deficit was substantial, and I know this is worrying to all members of this committee.
The prospect for 1960 is not very encouraging, either. The minister has made reference to the fact that the bill to be founded on this resolution will ask the house for authority to finance temporarily any deficit which may be incurred by the C.N.R. prior to the time this house can authorize payment of the actual ascertained deficit by a vote in the estimates. However, a review of the testimony of the officials of the C.N.R. given before the committee, plus an examination of the operating reports to date, is somewhat alarming. The deficit in 1959 was $43.5 million. The estimated deficit for 1960, when we were last officially informed, was given as $24 million. In other words it is indicated that in 1960 the net position of the C.N.R. might improve by $19.5 million. I believe the Minister of Finance in calculating his budget for the fiscal year has accepted the estimated figure of $24 million as the likely deficit of the C.N.R. for 1960.
However, we do have available since the sittings of the committee the net earnings report of the C.N.R. for the first four months of 1960. We find there that instead of showing a better net position compared to a like period in 1959, which I assume would be necessary if the company is to show an improvement in the over-all deficit of $19.5 million, we find that a deficit has already been incurred of $25 million compared with a deficit for the first four months of 1959 of $18.6 million. In other words the position is poorer for the first third of 1960 in relation to 1959 by $7.4 million.
It is very easy to calculate, if this trend continues in comparison with 1959 for the

Canadian National Railways balance of the fiscal year, what the result is likely to be. Three times $7.4 million comes to $22 million for a full year. Even if we were equalling rather than falling behind the record of last year, there would be a further deficit of $19.5 million beyond the estimated deficit of $24 million. In other words, when we project the poorer position which has been experienced this year and add the $19.5 million which would be required even to equal the position of last year, I calculate that those two figures come to $41 million. To put it in another way, if this continues the Minister of Finance will find that the position of the C.N.R. will require from him $41 million more than was the basis of his calculation when he predicted a $12 million surplus when he brought down his budget on March 31.
In view of the seriousness of this situation, I hope, the minister, either at this stage or on second reading, will give us some further information as to the prospects and as to any developments about which we may not have been informed which would in any way disparage the calculations I have presented to the committee. To sum these up briefly, even if we do as well as last year the calculations of the budget would be increased by another $19.5 million. If the trend we have experienced for four months should continue we would need an additional $22 million, so the budget would be out by $41 million.
It has been indicated that the capital budget this year will be down by some $56 million in comparison to 1959. Unfortunately, only two lines of typed reference were given in the committee relating to any proposals involving additional borrowing with respect to the proposals for increased terminal facilities at Toronto. We were only told in the committee that $6.6 million of this year's budget would be required for the Toronto terminal. However, hon. members know that we have on the agenda for debate today another resolution involving not only the $197.6 million to which reference is made in this resolution but an additional financing requirement of $100 million for the Canadian National Railways for a Toronto terminal.
The president of the railroad suggested that a very careful paring had been done with respect to the presentation of capital needs this year. He said that when the detailed statement of needs from the field was presented it amounted to $272.5 million. He told us there was a committee at Canadian National Railways headquarters which subsequently reviewed those proposals and the figure was brought down to $225.8 million. Then, he said, the proposals received the personal attention of himself as president and

of other officials at the head office, and there was a further reduction of $28.2 million.
What we should like to learn from the minister is this. After that stage what, if anything, in the way of examination and personal attention is given by the members of the cabinet, representing the shareholders, to ensure that this is the minimum figure which will be required for 1960 in view of the very unfavourable operating results that are reported? I found there was evidence given that last year, at approximately this date, the management discovered that it could do with some $40 million less than the figure presented to the cabinet and through the cabinet to parliament, as its 1959 capital requirement.
I think that decision was made in July. All hon. members will recognize that that date was not very far from the present date. I am wondering whether anything of that kind is contemplated this year, a further paring or a decision that certain expenditures will not be needed? If so, I think inquiries should be made now before the bill is drafted; because parliament should be given the most up-to-date calculation as to the minimum requirement. After all, the figures we are dealing with here were set up by the company perhaps four or five months ago. I think parliament should be taken a little more seriously than that year, when in June we are asked to pass certain capital expenditures and then within a matter of days afterwards a decision was reached by the C.N.R. that that figure could be reduced by the tremendous sum of $40-odd million.
The committee I think was disturbed, as indeed was the management of the road, by the very obvious growth in fixed charges. Reference is made to this item on page 65 of the committee report, where it is shown just how substantially fixed charges have risen since the last financial reorganization of the C.N.R., which affected the 1952 balance sheet, and it was indicated to us that from there the fixed charges would grow and would total approximately $80 million by 1965.
The other alarming feature of this-and this is all related to these substantial capital expenditures and borrowings-is that the percentage of revenues required to finance these fixed charges is also rising very substantially.
The Minister of Finance has always been one who, in connection with the increase in the national debt, has indicated that it is not too worrisome if it can be related to the growing national income, because when related to a percentage of the national income it does not show, in his view, an alarming growth. But that, of course, is not

similar to the predictions with respect to the fixed charges of the C.N.R. related to their anticipated income. I do not think we got from the committee as much as perhaps we should have, but as everybody knows we are badly rushed there; we put on three meetings a day, and these figures are very complicated, and the management is always in a hurry to get back to head office-

That is an understatement about management's hopes, I well know. In view of the seriousness of the financial forecast I believe we should get from the minister a statement of the progression of the fixed charges from 1952 forward rather than being satisfied with the figures we got from the committee, which as I recall them were really projected forward in part and were not projected back to 1952. I believe it would be worth while having them projected back to that year.
Another feature that is not generally understood by most of us, nor I am sure by a great number of the public at large, is the obligation under the 1951 financing act to which I referred earlier, that of the government to buy automatically preferred stock on the basis of a percentage of gross annual income. The amount of preferred stock under the reorganization of 1951 was set at $756 million. This involved a very substantial writing down from the past of the nominal book liabilities of the C.N.R. But I find that in only three years-1952, 1953 and 1955-was anything earned or available to pay anything on this 4 per cent preferred stock, and between 1952 and 1959 inclusive an additional $168 million of financing has been provided by this method quite apart from the aggregate of the deficits with which we are more familiar.
In 1959, in addition to meeting the deficit of $43 million through a vote of this house of $40 million, the government bought $22.1 million of preferred stock under this statute. In 1960 it is estimated that another $22 million will have to be provided through the purchase of preferred stock without any prospect, of course, of it providing for the nominal interest rate of 4 per cent.
As the Minister of Finance has indicated, we have in the past felt it necessary to peruse carefully the complicated figures such as he has given us this morning. I do not propose to make any extended remarks until I have an opportunity of examining the details of the proposals. Before closing the debate the minister might reiterate his intentions in this respect, but I understood him to say that the bill that will follow will contain this year a new provision. There was some noise in the chamber at the time and I did not
Canadian National Railways follow the minister with respect to certain financing forward to 1961 that apparently is to be incorporated in the new bill, but I will defer any comment on that point.

speechtext: I thank the minister for that explanation. I wonder if the committee would allow me a little indulgence. We are all acquainted with the voluminous nature of the reports of the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. For the benefit of the debate on second reading I should like to indicate to the committee a correction that should be made at page 138 of the sessional report. I am reported as having asked a question of Mr. Gordon in these words:

Do you know that this is made under the C.N.R. act?

That completes my reference to the committee report. Beyond that I simply want to say I have made subsequent inquiries and confirmed the belief 1 had when I asked the question there; that the economies under co-operation for which permission was being sought and to which reference was made in that instance were not made by the C.N.R. under the Railway Act but were in fact, as I had thought, made under the statute known as the C.N.R.-C.P.R. act.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there are several points in connection with the Canadian National financing that were touched on in the committee. There is one question on which I should like to ask the minister for

Canadian National Railways an explanation that none of us in the committee got around to asking for, although from a reading of the evidence it is very apparent that the question should have been asked, and it may be relevant to the point made by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River. At page 55 of the proceedings and evidence Mr. Drysdale asked this question:
Did the actual expenditures in 1959 coincide with the capital budget expenditures?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: No. I am going to mention that a little later. As a matter of fact, we considerably underspent our budget, for the reason that we started holding down on expenditures commencing July of last year.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: May I just refer to that? I have just looked at my notes. The committee will recognize that we were not informed either last Thursday night or Friday night that this item would come up for debate; we were not informed that it was coming up as the first item today until ten o'clock last night. Therefore I have had some difficulty in that interval in trying to refresh my memory about what went on in the committee. The hon. member is going to refer to the same subject that I was going to refer to. When I referred to the underspending decided upon in July, 1959 I used the figure $40 million. I think the hon. member for Port Arthur was just going to refer to the item that I see in my notes. The sum of $24.5 million is the correct figure, not $40 million.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: What is the page number?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: Page 57 of the proceedings and evidence.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
The question that comes to mind is why none of us asked why the C.N.R. decided last July to cut down. What I should like to ask the minister is, did he or any of his officials communicate with the Canadian National Railways and ask them to cut back and pare down their capital expenditures? If they did, it would seem reasonable and logical, I think, that he should give us a fuller explanation of how his department or he may be looking at the C.N.R. budget for this coming year.
If you search through the evidence you get the impression from Mr. Gordon's remarks that very strong efforts were made to cut down capital expenditures; that is, the projections for this year. I think he said that the estimates come from the field to head office, and they were trimmed $47 million in the first process at head office and then another $20 million before they were finally put in. I think we deserve to know whether this policy of cutting down on the capital expenditures is the result of advice or persuasion from the minister.


I can make this somewhat more relevant by underlining the fact that one of the expenditures for this coming year caused considerable controversy in the committee. It was not on a political basis necessarily. I refer to the expenditures to go into trucking operations. I will not say that there was a majority of the committee, but there was very strong objection on the part of certain members of the committee to the effect that the C.N.R. had no business getting into this field, or committing its capital budget to an extension into this particular field.
Another part of the capital expenditure comes to mind. The needs of the central traffic control program are now to be less in certain areas, since most of the work is completed. These expenditures are going down, but the revolutionary effect upon the communities resulting from those capital expenditures is just about to take place. Now, this is a step away from finance, but what bothers those of us who have divisional points in our constituencies-the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River knows this problem very well -is this. The people want to know why, when this dislocation takes place, proper provision is not made for relocation, for education, for training and this kind of thing. I am talking about something that is the result of capital expenditure; technically a revolution takes place in the employment picture of the railway community.
This, Mr. Chairman, is not immediately relevant to what the minister is bringing in here, but I should like to know whether in the consultations the minister may have had with the Canadian National Railways they were prepared at any time to make more extended provision than they have in their capital budget for education and retraining and relocation of personnel affected by the capital expenditure.
The question of the scale of the deficit is certainly great. From the figures that have come out so far this year the C.N.R. is not going to have as good a year in 1960 as it had in 1959. Certainly carloadings indicate that we are not going to get the optimistic trend that the lower deficit might indicate. I think the minister might pull together our ideas on this projected deficit and tell us what kind of estimate of business now appears available for this particular year. The president of the railway was relatively optimistic when he was before the committee, but certainly the figures that have come along since, in the past month, indicate that carloadings and revenue are not going up to the degree that was expected.
There is one other question on which I should like an answer from the minister.

Mr. Gordon, at page 56 of the proceedings and evidence, gives an indication that the company expects to recoup, I take it, approximately $10 million from the St. Lawrence seaway authority for expenditures incurred in constructing the diversion and related facilities around the Victoria bridge.
I think this is a large enough sum for us to be given an indication as to whether that money is going to be coming to the Canadian National Railways this particular year.
The whole question over the past decade in the financing of the Canadian National Railways would seem to be that the government by rather large capital expenditures has been trying to put the Canadian National Railways in a position to modernize and so eventually reach the state of balancing its budget and becoming a more viable concern. Despite all the optimism of the president of the Canadian National Railways-and I am not going to argue that this expenditure should not have been made-the railway is in no better position that we can see, relative to what it was five or six years ago, as a result of all this expenditure.
The capital program is going to continue on a very large scale until 1965, and this raises one point. Surely the Canadian National Railways and the government of Canada have been wrong or, let us say, mistaken in their projection into the future. If we go back five years when very large capital expenditures on the C.T.C. and on dieseliza-tion and all that sort of thing were being undertaken, the argument was that those expenditures would enable the railway to get into a viable economic position. Now the expenditures have been made. I understand the last steam locomotive has blown its whistle on the Canadian National Railways, and the railway is not in any better position.
I know the president argues that despite increases in productivity, this situation has been created by wage demands and changes in the transportation picture, especially the increasing amount of traffic that is hauled by rival carriers. But my point is that the projection has been wrong; it has been mistaken.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
The hon. member has conceded that as against the savings which were projected and which I understand have been made, it was not foreseen that there would be adverse elements which have affected the situation. Would it not be fair for him to assess those, because after all we are not prophets and cannot have all the wisdom in the world. If in fact savings were actually
Canadian National Railways made though offset by unforeseen and even keener competition from rival methods of carriage, is it not fair to take that into account?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I certainly agree with the hon. member that it must be taken into account, but my whole point is that where you are expending millions and millions of dollars, substantial fractions of billions of dollars, very careful projections need to be made, and all I am suggesting is that within five years the optimistic projections have been proved wrong. The program is now going to continue for another five years, and I am just wondering what assurances we will have that there is more accuracy in the present projections.
Put in its most simple terms, a tremendous amount of capital has been pumped into Canadian National Railways since the war to make it a going concern. Yet in 1960 the C.N.R. seems no closer to being a going concern than it was in the post-war years up to a decade ago. Surely this faces us with a question of economics and a question as to the future. No one is in a position to say that this should end the C.N.R. We cannot turn our backs on the problem, but I do think we should know much more concretely and have a much tighter projection as to the future of this railway in terms of deficits. I cannot see why these trends toward loss of traffic to rival carriers and the trends as to wage demands were not taken into the picture.
Looking back over the years it seems to me that the C.N.R. repeatedly comes before the house committee and these bills are brought before the house, and the projection is always too short range and always too optimistic. I am not suggesting that we should call a halt to passing measures such as this, but certainly we should get a much clearer pattern as to where we are going in our railway expenditure. This raises an issue that is much larger than what is now before this house, and that is the issue before the royal commission on transportation. I want to emphasize that I do not believe the royal commission on transportation is getting to the nub of problems such as this. I feel that its proceedings have developed into an argument between various regions of the country over questions involving the freight rate structure, which is very complicated and which only a few experts can understand. I do not know what Solomons there are on the royal commission on transportation, but I do not envy them the task of working out the freight rates question.
It seems to me that what we have to consider is something even more important than anything the royal commission is trying to settle, namely where this railway is heading

Canadian National Railways when we keep on having these huge deficits when, despite the immense expenditures, the railway that we are supporting is not improving its position. Mr. Gordon has told us to fire him if we do not think he is efficient. I am not yet at the stage where I wish to suggest that we should importune the government to fire Mr. Gordon, but I certainly think we have to take into consideration whether we can go on much longer with the present management of the railway and the present treatment that the government is giving to the railway, and yet year after year be faced with this very dark financial picture.
It would seem to me that it would be acceptable if we took it for granted-this of course is what the members of this party believe-that the government-owned railway is not a viable economic concern in the sense of a corporation operating in a free market structure, but it is very hard to get this view generally accepted not only in the minds of members of parliament but outside the house. The president of Canadian National Railways insists that his railway be treated like any other corporation. That is one of the reasons he refuses to give members of parliament certain information they would like to have. In other words, the president of Canadian National Railways insists that this is a corporation like any other corporation, and one that is operating under many of the same factors. As I say, he goes so far as to say that we should fire the management if we think they are inefficient. What can one help but think about the management if after these tremendous capital expenditures, with many more to go, the picture is still as stark and gloomy as ever?
I should like to argue that Mr. Gordon himself and those who expect Canadian National Railways to operate like any other corporation, for example the Canadian Pacific Railway, are the ones who are mistaken. I think the president himself has a wrong conception of the role of this corporation. I think it is time we stopped kidding ourselves that by bills such as this, that pump millions into the C.N.R. structure for capital improvement, we are finally going to enable the railway to reach the stage where it will show a balance sheet with profits. In the light of our experience with the C.N.R. over the last 10 years it almost seems to me that the balance sheet is not a very important item at all. This leads me to the suggestion that what we should perhaps do is analyse just how far we want to go as a government and as a nation in committing ourselves to Canadian National Railways, and also just what we expect from the railway.
It seems to be ironical that we should allow the president of Canadian National


Railways to go before the royal commission on transportation and present his argument on the statutory grain rates, for example, or his argument so far as the trucking situation is concerned; or that we should allow Canadian National Railways to appear before the royal commission as an independent organization, when we know that the government is underwriting the railway and that in many ways the railway is carrying out chores which can never be economical in terms of the balance sheet but which the government and the people of Canada expect it to do.
I know that one of the things we expect in our part of the country is that when the iron ore trenches north of lake Superior are opened up, Canadian National Railways will be in there to provide rail service. What I am suggesting is that we expect much more from Canadian National Railways than we can expect from an ordinary corporation operating in a free market. For this reason the attitude of the president and of the government tends to be out of line. We are importing into our consideration of Canadian National Railways arguments, attitudes and financial procedures that apply to a free market corporation, and that is not what we have.
I should like to have the minister's comments upon this particular situation. It seems to me that if the future of Canadian National Railways is not to be a black one, you must forget the idea it is an organization primarily designed to make a profit. If the members of this house believe it is the primary design of Canadian National Railways to make a profit, then it seems to me we have to come to grips with Canadian National Railways and do some real cutting and slashing. We have to get much tougher than we have been. It certainly seems to me that Canadian National, judged as a corporation in the free market, has been a failure in the last five or six years. I am not going to be the one to call for Mr. Gordon's head, but some of the members of the house who are much more wedded to the free enterprise concept should be pressuring the government at this time, it seems to me, to have Mr. Gordon's head.
We will support this resolution, Mr. Chairman. However, I should like to underline again that the understanding members of parliament have of the operations of Canadian National Railways on the financial side is of a sketchy nature. This year Mr. Gordon, before the committee, tried a new approach in order to enlighten us on the railway's problems. Instead of reading from reports he showed us a series of graphs and charts. This was much better than the form of presentation used in the past. The difficulty with

this presentation, however, was that questions and analyses are rather difficult in a darkened room when graphs are flying on and off a board. I think anyone who reads the evidence from approximately page 36 through to about page 70 is going to come to the conclusion that our analysis of the finances of Canadian National Railways was rather superficial. I believe our analysis of this resolution in this committee is probably going to be superficial, and for that reason I should like to throw the committee upon the mercy of the Minister of Finance. Perhaps with that prodigious industry of his-he has spent so much time understanding the finances of the government and the Canadian National -he could give us some enlightenment on these points, especially the ones brought up by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River. Perhaps he could enlighten us on this whole question of the government's views on the Canadian National and its efficiency.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I want to raise a matter which I raised in the committee on railways, air lines and shipping and which caused a good deal of discussion at that time, although we did not seem to get too many answers. I refer to the entry of the railroads into the trucking business. I think this is something that needs to be given very serious consideration. We were told by Mr. Gordon in that committee that the railroad had committed $5 million to the purchase of trucking firms, and that they were asking for a further $5 million this year. At that time I suggested that before the second $5 million was committed we should be made aware of what had been done with the first $5 million.
It was my feeling that if the railroad went too extensively into the trucking business it might have the effect of lessening competition in the transportation field, and I do not believe that would be in the public interest. I should like to cite a case which came up in 1957, and which would indicate to some extent the value of having trucking competition with the railroads. I refer to a submission made to the board of transport commissioners at a time when the railroads had made some rather serious cuts in their rates. This quotation is taken from the submission made to the board of transport commissioners by the Canadian trucking association, and the rate cuts referred to are taken from the published tariffs of the Canadian National and Canadian Pacific railways, which are identical. Paragraph 2 of this brief says:
It can be seen most of the rate reductions are of the order of 40 per cent and more, some even exceed 70 per cent and one represents a cut of 77 per cent.
Canadian National Railways
I believe that these benefits accrue directly from competition in the transportation field. There is little doubt in my mind that no such rate cuts would have been made if the railroads had owned these particular trucking companies. I feel that anybody can see the need for the railroads to have feeder lines today to bring goods to the railroads. However, when we tried to find out in the committee on railways, air lines and shipping what the policy of the Canadian National was going to be in going into the trucking business, there were some rather interesting answers given by Mr. Gordon in reply to the hon. member for Simcoe North. I do not want to take up too much of the time of the committee so I will not read the question, but I will read Mr. Gordon's answer, which is self-explanatory. At page 132 of the evidence of that committee Mr. Gordon is reported as saying:
We have had quite a number of operators who have offered themselves for sale. What we are trying to do now, and we are at a very early stage, is to pick and choose in such a way so that we will form a backbone of trucking service which will be on a coast to coast basis. We may select any particular trucking operation which might fit into that plan; but we do not want to duplicate or overlap.
Then the hon. member for Simcoe North said:
I do not quite understand why you want coast to coast trucking service. I seem to be a little confused on that subject. It would seem to me that you would be more interested in providing a trucking service which would truck, say, within a metropolitan area and thereby generate coast to coast shipping for your railway.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Because there are many instances where the traffic that is operating under modern conditions is not best handled by the railway.
It seems to me this only indicates the railway's desire to go completely into that line of endeavour, thereby eliminating competition. We had another instance of the lack of competition given to us in the committee, and that was in the piggyback operations of the railroad. We were informed by Mr. Gordon that in the maritime provinces the railroad would not take trucks belonging to anybody else in the piggyback operation; they would take only their own trucks and refuse to carry trucks belonging to anyone else. I feel it is significant that, notwithstanding the Maritime Freight Rates Act, freight rates have gone up faster in the maritimes in the past 10 years than in other parts of Canada. I suggest to the committee this is the result of lack of competition.
I do not know what effect the amount of money the railroad has spent has had in the way of lessening competition, but it seems to me it is a wrong policy for the railroad to commit $5 million to this purpose and not tell

Canadian National Railways parliament what they have done with that amount of money. Now they are asking for a further $5 million and I see that according to the terms of this resolution the railroad could enter into contracts up until July 31, 1961. It seems to me we should have some idea of what has been done so that we can make some assessment of whether this purchase of truck lines by the railroad is going to have the effect of lessening competition. I do not see what other effect it could have.
In the past, royal commissions on transportation have said there should not be too much concern in that regard because it was very easy to get into and out of the trucking business. The cost was small and, therefore, it would be very hard to eliminate competition. However, the trucking industry has been growing in importance in the last few years. Costs have risen greatly. Some of the types of trucks that are used in the kind of competition referred to here would cost $25,000, $30,000 or even up to $40,000 per unit. It is not quite as easy to start in this business as it was a number of years ago. Second, there is a great deal more control by provincial governments. One has to prove public necessity before a licence is granted to operate a trucking business. I suggest that if the railroad applied for a trucking licence in an area in which there was room for only one trucking firm, the provincial government would be hesitant about granting a licence for another person to go into competition with the railroad. Then we would be in the position of having no competition whatsoever in those areas. We would have a railroad owned trucking operation competing with the railway, and I do not think that would be a very effective means of competition. As I said before, I do not think we would have had the rate cuts we have had if it had not been for the advent of trucking competition.
I suggest to the government that this whole question be referred to the royal commission on transportation. I have little doubt that it will come before them, but I think there should be a direction from the government to the royal commission that it is their feeling that this whole matter should be completely investigated, and I think we should have a report from the royal commission before the railroad is allowed to go too much further into this field.

I wish the minister would explain exactly when is it that the C.N.R. obtains its money from the money market on its own initiative and when it obtains it by way of loans from the minister. I notice that this resolution calls for a measure to


grant the minister authority to make additional loans to Canadian National Railways. The money market was rather swamped last year when there was a most unexpected demand on it by Canadian National Railways for $300 million, I believe it was, which is a large amount. I am glad that the issue was oversubscribed at the time; I understand the response to the offering of Canadian National Railways was excellent indeed.

speechtext: Highest interest rates ever.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Yes, I realize the interest rates were excessive. However, it indicated a little loosening up at the time of available resources in the investment field. At that time we were a little amazed because it was our understanding that these capital needs of the C.N.R. would be made available by the minister. I believe he had received the authority to make this money available to Canadian National Railways, and then rather unexpectedly and for reasons which the minister has not yet explained in this house Canadian National Railways appealed to the money market on its own.
The minister is again asking for authority to make available to Canadian National Railways moneys not exceeding in total $203,950,000. I wonder whether we might have some assurance from the minister that he has every intention of making this money available, or whether, if and when the minister may find himself in difficult circumstances, Canadian National Railways will again have to approach the market on its own. I believe this committee is entitled to a clarification of what happened last year and why it happened, and also an explanation of what are the intentions of the government with regard to implementing the resolution now before us.
The other issue I would like to raise is this. Last year there was indication that the development program of Canadian National Railways was being deliberately curtailed by orders of the government in order to help the government arrive at a balanced budget. I know this could not be so because any curtailment of expansion of the C.N.R. would have nothing to do with the balancing of the budget; there is no relationship at all. However, there is a relationship between expansion and inflation, the availability of investment resources on the money market and the issue of unemployment.
I regret that that expansion program of Canadian National Railways was curtailed, thereby aiding and abetting the unemployment situation. I regret especially that the Canadian National Railways expansion program was not able to even absorb the numbers who were laid off by the railway company

because of automation. I believe that in that one-year period Canadian National Railways laid off some 13,000 men. When there is a great expansion program under way and men with 18 years of seniority have to be laid off, as has happened, then I feel it is most unwise for the government to curtail the plans and expansion needs of Canadian National Railways.
This happened last year, and I think the country is entitled to an explanation as to why that planned program was curtailed. Was it in order to help contain inflation? Was it because of lack of resources, of capital? 1 would like to know whether it is the intention of the government to contain the dangers of inflation and restore normal levels of supply and demand to the money market, even if it means greatly increased unemployment. I would also like to know whether the government regards full employment as an expendable factor when a decision has to be made in this regard. We are afraid, and many of the working people of Canada are becoming increasingly afraid also, that when the government makes a decision on this matter the welfare of the Canadian worker is considered as the expendable element, and that he has to pay the penalty of unemployment in order to help the government achieve other admittedly worth-while objectives.
I hope the minister will be able to make a reply on this matter of financing and also the matter of when curtailment of the program is in order and when it is not.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I would like to make a few remarks, Mr. Chairman, before this resolution is approved. As a member of the committee which reviewed the budget reports of the C.N.R., in the writing of our report I think for the first time since the government changed we did make mention of the fact that we were concerned about the continuing deficits of the C.N.R.
With regard to some of the remarks made by the hon. member for Port Arthur, it is my opinion that the C.N.R. should be operated on the same basis as the C.P.R., and that is to provide services at a reasonable cost, and to get themselves into the black and stay in the black.
One of the recommendations made by the committee had to do with the board of directors. In this regard I was very interested in the report of the Canadian Pacific Railway. They have 24 members on the board of directors of whom seven are on the executive committee, compared to the Canadian National Railways where they have seven members on the board of directors only two of whom are the executive committee.
In testimony the president pointed out that he and any two directors formed the
Canadian National Railways executive committee. The function of the executive committee, of course, is to approve the acts of the president in the administration of the railway. The president was careful to point out that the C.P.R. stands on its own feet, that it is a private corporation and not under the control of the government. That is all very fine, but because of that attitude figures and facts and questions about the operation of the railroad were not given that full disclosure with which they should have been treated.
The C.N.R. is not in that position whatsoever. The C.N.R. is in the favoured position of having all the advantages of free enterprise and having none of the disadvantages. When they have a deficit to whom do they come? They come to the government. But the government has no real control over the C.N.R. As the minister himself pointed out, he simply reports to parliament on behalf of the company. Indeed, the committee was told about a statement by Right Hon. Mr. Mackenzie Kang when the C.N.R. was set up, making it clear that the company was to be operated as a private enterprise corporation over which the government would have no direct control. So we have this private enterprise corporation functioning without the checks and controls which government could place on management, and without the checks and controls which are normally placed on a business enterprise by shareholders and by outside competition under free enterprise.
The evidence makes it clear that the directors do not take an active interest in the operation of the railroad. In one case they stated themselves that they were not too conversant with the details. On the other hand, when one looks at the Canadian Pacific Railway one finds an entirely different setup which characterizes the whole operation, from the board of directors to the final balance sheet. I wish the balance sheets of the C.N.R. bore some resemblance to the balance sheets of the C.P.R.
I return to the point I wish to make, which is that to all intents and purposes the president of the C.N.R. does not have those checks and balances on his power or his decisions which one finds either in a corporation which is controlled directly by the government or in a corporation which is controlled by a board of directors responsible to the shareholders, and I do not think that is the best arrangement for a good operation.
I do not wish to belabour this point. All one has to do is read the reports of the C.N.R. Look at the money that has been poured into it since the end of the war, some $500 million. Then take a look at the final

Canadian National Railways figure for each year. They are shown as far back as 1935, but let us go back simply to 1950. It will be seen that the over-all deficit amounts to something in the neighbourhood of $160 million, while the operation of another railroad, which does perhaps have certain advantages, shows a reasonably good picture.
I am viewing this question simply from the point of view of a free enterprise economy. I do not think the C.N.R. is a make-work program. I think it is in the same position as the C.P.R., and that it is intended to provide a service at a reasonable cost. I say there is something that we should look into with regard to C.N.R. operations. There must come an end to these continuing large scale deficits. Some measure of government action will eventually have to be taken unless the railroad can clear its own house and pull itself into a more reasonable condition.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I should like to make one or two brief comments on this subject. I am particularly interested in a matter concerning which the hon. member for Vancouver-Kings-way has spoken, and that is the activity of the C.N.R. in the trucking field. As the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway pointed out, there was considerable questioning of Mr. Gordon on this particular subject.
In the budget of 1959 some $15 million was allocated to enable the C.N.R. to get into the trucking field. Of that $15 million the company has apparently used $5 million. The committee endeavoured to find out how this money was being spent. Mr. Gordon indicated that the majority of the deals had not been consummated, and he thought it was not in the interests of the C.N.R. to have the names of the trucking firms revealed at this particular time. I endeavoured to have Mr. Gordon indicate to the committee what was the long range objective of the C.N.R. with regard to the trucking field, and I suggested that if it were not possible to reveal the names at least he could indicate to the committee how the money was to be spent. Unfortunately I did not get an answer to this particular question.
What worries me is that this question is very important to the Canadian people generally, as was underlined during the recent discussion of the Combines Investigation Act. When a government entity such as the C.N.R. is able to expand into the field of trucking, and members of parliament are not told the extent to which this move is likely to go, a serious position arises. There was $5 million allocated for this purpose in 1959. That has been taken up. There is to be another $5 million allocated in 1960, and there is every

reason to believe there will be a further $5 million spent for the same purpose.
I think it is important to examine at this time, in some detail, whether an expansion of this kind is in the public interest. I must admit readily that I think what Mr. Gordon is doing is in the interests of the C.N.R. His main objective is to cut the deficit, and anything he can do in that direction is very commendable as far as the C.N.R. is concerned. However, we do not know what effect this is going to have on the remainder of the Canadian economy. We are being left in the dark about these transactions, and what worries me is that by the time the money has been allocated-perhaps over a period of three years, if the $15 million is spent-the C.N.R. may have bought out the major trucking companies across Canada and, in effect, stifled trucking competition. The answer given by the C.N.R. to our inquiries in the committee has been "We do not think it is in the interests of the C.N.R. at this time to disclose the information".
However, during the committee proceedings I was in a position to ask Mr. Gordon when he thought he would be in a position to indicate what interests had been acquired by the C.N.R. I am reading from the minutes of the committee proceedings at page 222.

I was asked then, Mr. Chairman, as to whether I had communicated with the Canadian National Railways management concerning the program of capital investment in 1959. Was the wicked Minister of Finance somehow responsible for imposing his ideas upon the management of
Canadian National Railways the C.N.R. and staying their hand in undertaking useful capital expenditures?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: "Wicked" is the minister's own word.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Perhaps that is the way I have grown accustomed to looking upon myself in this role. I can disclaim at once having had any communication with the management of Canadian National Railways in this respect. The decisions in regard to capital expenditures made by the management in 1959 were their own decisions. It will be clear to those who have followed the evidence heard in the committee that the result of the fact that capital expenditures were not as large as they were in the preceding year has been only to delay some of the expenditures; because, as the president of Canadian National Railways pointed out at page 57 of the evidence, the effect has been, of course, to create some budgetary pressures this year.
The next question raised was concerning the recovery of a claim of Canadian National Railways in respect of the construction work on the St. Lawrence waterway arising out of a railway diversion there. I have no further information on that point. I understand that the amount has not been recovered yet, but the committee will recall Mr. Gordon's firm assertion to the committee at page 57 of the proceedings that the company's claim was valid, right, legal and moral, and he indicated his confidence that the claim would be recovered.
I was asked by one hon. member concerning the market borrowings of Canadian National Railways and the course of borrowings from the Minister of Finance. Provision is made in this annual legislation for the financing of Canadian National Railways. Authorization is given to the Minister of Finance to extend loans to the company, and provision is also made for public borrowing on the market.
When we came into office in 1957 we found there had not been any market issue on the part of the C.N.R. for some very considerable time. Indeed, we found that the C.N.R. had borrowed something like $400 million from the treasury and no effort had been made, certainly no sufficient effort, to liquidate that indebtedness to the treasury by borrowing through a public issue of bonds. Since that time we have provided out of the treasury for the current needs of Canadian National Railways, but the company has at intervals of approximately one year undertaken a market offering with a view to liquidating in whole or in part that indebtedness to the treasury.

Canadian National Railways
That is the course that has been followed. The timing, the amounts, the terms of these offerings are a matter of consultation between the management of the company and the Minister of Finance. I think it is a matter of some satisfaction that a high degree of success has been attained in connection with these offerings of Canadian National Railways. The government, of course, must be consulted in these matters, because these bonds of the company are offered only with a guarantee by the Minister of Finance on behalf of the government.
The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam suggested that the last offering was a great surprise. I do not know on what authority the hon. gentleman makes a statement like that. Certainly within the ordinary decisions of selection and timing in these matters, I think everyone was well aware that there had not been an offering of C.N.R. bonds for approximately one year, and that the pattern that had been followed indicated that these offerings were being made at intervals of approximately one year.
I was invited also to give some projection on a long range basis of the future policy and future financial position of Canadian National Railways. I must modestly at once assert that that is rather a tall order to put to anyone. This is going to depend upon many factors, factors related to the economic growth of the country, to the preferences of the public, to the broad direction of economic growth and change and also those questions which go to the root of the whole basis of the outlook for railway transportation in general in the future. There are so many factors that enter into the situation and qualify anything one might say in this respect that I do not think it would be profitable to attempt to read the future in that regard for very long at a time.
Mr. Chairman, may I call it one o'clock?
At one o'clock the committee took recess.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the last subject that I was making comment upon was the request that I endeavour to give some long range projection of the future course of the operations, business outlook and finance of Canadian National Railways. This is a subject that is engaging the attention of the best minds in Canadian National Railways. I have indicated reasons why it is difficult to be precise in a field of this kind very far into the future. This is a field that


is undergoing very rapid change, as anyone who has followed the history of railway operations over the past couple of decades well knows.
Mention was made also of what were described as limitations on the annual review of the operations of the Canadian National system. Well, the thought that immediately came to my mind was this, Mr. Chairman. There is very full opportunity available to hon. members of the house through the appointment of the committee that is set up annually for this purpose. This year the committee sat for four consecutive days, namely March 28, 29, 30 and 31. Those were lengthy sessions that the committee held. I do not know of any large corporation engaged in private enterprise which is submitted at its annual meeting to a four-day examination of the details of its business, the way this crown corporation and its subsidiary, Trans-Canada Air Lines, are. The annual meetings of most of the large corporations in this country, which are comparable in size and extent with the Canadian National Railway's operations, last normally for not more than half a day. This is not to suggest that there should not be fuller examination, if any hon. member on that committee wishes, into the affairs of Canadian National Railways. I am simply pointing out that probably the affairs of Canadian National Railways, at the hands of this committee established annually by the house for the purpose, receive a fuller and more searching examination than the comparable affairs of any similar corporation engaged in private enterprise in this country.
If any hon. member has not obtained all the information he sought in that committee it is not possible for me to take any responsibility in that respect. One must remember, of course, Mr. Chairman-and I think this is the point that has been raised by the representatives of management of Canadian National Railways in appearing before the committee-that after all they are engaged in competition with another transcontinental railway, namely the Canadian Pacific Railway. They are also engaged in competition with trucking interests and other forms of transportation; therefore they feel that, in relation to some detailed aspects of their business, to give fuller information would be to make available to their competitors information which could be used to the detriment of the system.
Now, here is a problem in balance, the problem on the one hand of affording to the elected representatives of the people the fullest information concerning the operations and finances of a crown corporation, and on the

other hand seeking to protect the competitive position of that company in relation to its competitors.
I think the final subject that was raised concerns the entry of Canadian National Railways into trucking operations. This has been referred to by several hon. members from British Columbia. This, Mr. Chairman, if we ever embarked upon it, could prove to be a very large subject, and I think it would be unprofitable to us here and now to attempt to discuss it broadly or enter upon the time-honoured debate as between railway operations and trucking operations. I have had some long experience with this subject, Mr. Chairman, and I think I have some appreciation of its extent and ramifications.
The fact is that the railways of this country over long years have been engaged in other forms of transportation than rail operations. The Canadian Pacific has operated a system of steamships; Canadian National Railways for a time also operated a steamship service. Both companies are engaged in air operations, and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company has been engaged in trucking operations in some forms for some years. It was this fact which led Canadian National Railways to represent to the government, something like a year and a half ago, that in order to protect their competitive position vis-a-vis the Canadian Pacific system, and also their position in the face of competition from truckers, it would be necessary for them to enter into trucking operations to some extent.
The committee will recall that a year ago the plan of Canadian National Railways to invest a total of $15 million in the acquisition of trucking rights and operations was discussed and approved. This year the committee was informed by the management of Canadian National Railways that during the past year the company had undertaken commitments in relation to the acquisition of trucking rights and facilities amounting to $5 million. The 1960 budget of the company contemplates the expenditure of a further $5 million for this purpose.
Mr. Donald Gordon, as some hon. members pointed out this morning, indicated why he felt he should not be pressed to give the committee particulars as to the contracts the company had entered into for the acquisition of trucking rights and interests. I am not in a position to give the committee any further information in that regard at this time. In any event, I think the house would normally expect to receive information of that type through the Minister of Transport rather than through the Minister of Finance. But when these negotiations are completed and
Canadian National Railways the particular trucking lines are acquired, I presume the president of Canadian National Railways would not then maintain the objection he expressed in the committee to giving details. I understand that he was protecting the position of the company in pending negotiations, or in any event protecting the position of the company until these various purchases had been consummated.
A question was raised about the C.N.R. acquiring transcontinental trucking services. It was pointed out by several hon. members this morning that this did not look like using trucks as feeders to a railway system. No, it does not, Mr. Chairman. As I understand what Mr. Donald Gordon was saying in this respect, it was that there are certain types of traffic that are moving even transcontinentally by truck, with respect to which the railways do not find themselves in an effective position to compete with the trucking operations because of the advantages of flexibility that rest with the trucks. It was with a view to putting the Canadian National system in a position to compete with these services that, as I read his evidence, Mr. Donald Gordon was indicating that the company might wish to establish transcontinental services as distinguished from services that might be regarded as feeders to normal rail operations.
I believe the house is well aware that both railway companies have used trucking services very effectively as feeders to their rail services, and they have maintained-I have no doubt that in this respect they are on sound ground-that apart from providing such trucking services they are not in a position to compete effectively against truckers for certain classes of traffic.
I think the final aspect of this matter that was raised was whether there might be any question of suppression of competition if a company like Canadian National embarked more extensively into the field of trucking operations and bought up existing services. I do not think anyone need have any fears about lack of competition in transportation in Canada. This is a very highly competitive field. Indeed, there has been an intensification of competition in this field in the last quarter century that has left the railways in a position where, working under severe regulation as they have been, they have maintained that they are prevented from protecting their position in the face of new forms of competitive transportation. So these are all considerations that have entered into the decision of the management of Canadian National Railways to enter the trucking field, and the reasons the present bill, which is related to the budget for 1960, contemplates the investment of a further $5 million in the acquisition of trucking rights and facilities.

Canadian National Railways
Because answers in detail on certain negotiations were not available to this year's committee does not mean, as I interpret the evidence, that information of that kind would not be available next year after negotiations are completed with respect to contracts which were under negotiation or had not yet been consummated at the time the committee was sitting in March last.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to refer first to the last point dealt with by the minister, namely the type of information requested by a couple of other members of the committee from Vancouver. I think one of them quoted some reference in the proceedings to what I had said, but I want to assure the minister that I was endeavouring to lend some help to the president of the road if, from the competitive point of view, a short period of time was required before giving this information. But I think all members of the committee will agree that that concession having been made in the committee, and the fact that the point was not pursued, gave the committee the very definite understanding that there was a commitment that before we passed this legislation we would find the Minister of Transport in his seat ready to give this information. He is not here today, but perhaps he could be here on second reading of the bill, inasmuch as there was a definite understanding that the legislation could not be expected to receive passage in the house with the approval of most hon. members unless this information was provided.
I do not think it was quoted by hon. members who spoke on this subject this morning but I believe a point was reached in the proceedings-I cannot put my finger on the passage at the moment-where the president indicated that if pressed he would even give the information then. Certainly we all got the impression that there was a commitment so far as the president was concerned. I think he was grateful for the extra two months for negotiation, but he did not expect the legislation would pass without giving the information to parliament which supplies these funds.
Before we approve the resolution there is another point on which I should like a little more information from the minister. When he rose to reply he said he had obtained the impression from the debate that he was being characterized again as the wicked Minister of Finance. I certainly do not think that is the impression he has conveyed today. If he is to be criticized at all, I think he might be criticized on the grounds of extraordinary benevolence and complacency.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: I was referring to the suggestion that there had been some interference on the part of the Minister of Finance with the operations of the management of Canadian National Railways in relation to its capital investment program.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Quite; and it is on that point that I wonder whether the committee will not come to the conclusion that the minister and his department are perhaps not checking on these matters sufficiently. I raised the point originally that last year, within a few days after we had been considering legislation identical with the legislation we are considering now, the C.N.R. came to the conclusion that an amount of $241 million in the funds that parliament had been asked to provide a few days earlier was not going to be necessary. I raised the question this morning whether the same kind of thing would happen this year.
I have more reason to raise the question about this year's budget. I failed to draw this to the attention of this committee this morning but I recall that in the sessional committee on railways, air lines and shipping owned by the government the president himself said, although I do not think he put a dollar value on it, that the budget included an item for 40 diesel locomotives which might not be required this year.
I indicated in my main remarks this morning that the operating experience, as reported for the first four months, has been very disappointing indeed. The road is not even equalling the equivalent net revenue position of 1959. Indeed, in the first four months it has gone behind the experience of 1959 to the extent of $7.5 million. I just cannnot imagine the minister being so indifferent to this situation that he or his officers would overlook this suggestion of the Canadian National that this item might not be required; and inasmuch as the budget has been prepared many months ago, I would think that before a bill was prepared for parliament the minister would scrutinize the capital requirements again and ask whether or not there are to be reductions such as were made a few days after this legislation was passed last year. I would think he would ask in particular whether the report to parliament, along the lines indicated by the president of the road, was in accordance with the circumstances, and whether it is going to be necessary in 1960 to provide financing for these 40 diesel units to which reference was made on page 55 of the report of the committee on railways, air lines and shipping.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, our information is that this capital program is required. The hon. member speaks about this

program having been prepared many, many months ago. It is not quite that long, Mr. Chairman. It is true that work on the preparation of the annual budget, as regards both capital expenditures and current operations, is begun before the end of the previous year, but this type of document is under examination in the early months of the succeeding year and the house has had an opportunity, through the committee, to obtain any recent information on the subject. It was in line with the situation at the end of March that the committee examined the budget and proposed capital expenditures for 1960. I do not profess to have anything new, anything different, anything to vary the picture as disclosed to the committee of this house by the management of Canadian National Railways.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
This information was provided on March 28. Many millions of dollars are involved. The remarks of the president of the road on March 28, to which I referred on page 55 of the minutes, read as follows:
We have a commitment item in the 1960 budget for an additional 40 units, for which commitment authority was previously granted, but these locomotives will be purchased only if traffic should exceed our expectations in the latter part of 1960 or during 1961.
Surely, with money for any purpose being as scarce as it is, the parliament of this country would expect the minister and his officers, after two months from the receipt of this type of information and before asking us for unnecessary authority, to make inquiry and try to determine whether, having regard to the operating results which are very depressing, this commitment need be made by this parliament in the bill that will follow this resolution.
