maintopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
There is, in my riding, an organized trucking service operating in areas not served by the railways.
Today, after years of difficulties, private interests have managed to set up a service which is entirely satisfactory to their customers.
Now that the operation is soundly established, railway companies want to set up a trucking service of their own.
We know that, for years the C.N.R. has been unable to take care of its own expenditures and that every year it requires government subsidies to meet its operating costs. Well, if for the sole purpose of competing with existing services, the railway puts in a trucking business which cannot meet its
Canadian National Railways own expenditures-as is already the case for its railroad operations-are we not justified in wondering whether, sooner or later, the government will not be faced with the obligation of supplying new grants to cover more losses in that respect?
If the railways are allowed to enter that field, our truckers and private trucking companies will sustain losses that will be too much for them, and will have no other alternative than to apply for government grants to make up for their deficits.
In my opinion, Mr. Chairman, it would not be to the government's advantage to encourage railways to establish trucking operations, especially in areas where there are no railroads and where there will probably never be any.
If private concerns or interests have been successful in providing the transportation needs of any given area, I fail to see why railways should be allowed to compete with them.
Therefore, I am all in favour of the suggestion made by the hon. member for Van-couver-Kingsway (Mr. Browne) and I move that the matter of highway transportation be referred to a royal commission on transport.
(Text):

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: I just wanted to ask the minister if he could give us any indication as to whether the amount of money being extended by the Canadian National to Trans-Canada Air Lines is the same as was indicated in the annual report of Trans-Canada Air Lines, namely approximately $82 million for this coming year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: There is no information to change that indication, Mr. Chairman, since the matter was before the committee. This figure is largely influenced by the requirement of Trans-Canada Air Lines in relation to the purchase of new equipment.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
On page 365 of the committee report we find the Trans-Canada Air Lines property and equipment budget for 1960, 1961 and 1962, and we have a rather remarkable cut-down in major construction as you get past 1960. When you look at Canadian National Railways chart No. 14, page 62, which was displayed to us by the president of the C.N.R., you get an indication that there is going to be a rather remarkable cut-down in capital expenditures, although we did get an indication that the fixed charges were going to go up for a number of years until they hit a peak at some $70

Canadian National Railways million. This is the sort oi projection which I was talking about, which would be very useful.
I am wondering what the attitude or position of the government is going to be with regard to making absolutely sure these projections are carried out. What guarantee have we that we are going to get this continued cut-down in these rather large expenditures? Can we assume that Canadian National Railways and Trans-Canada Air Lines are entering a decade in which their capital needs will be such, no matter what difficulties either one of these lines may get into, that we can absolutely count on the fact that this is going to continue on its downward path?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Unfortunately there are wide fluctuations from year to year in the capital requirements of Trans-Canada Air Lines. The figures appearing on page 365 of the proceedings of the committee for the years 1960, 1961 and 1962 very clearly illustrate this fact. It happens that in 1960 Trans-Canada Air Lines is taking delivery of a great deal of new equipment. Their program arises out of re-equipment of their principal lines of operation, and that equipment is being delivered in 1960. Then largely with the completion of that program their requirements for 1961 and 1962 will be very materially reduced.
It is of course unfortunate from the financing point of view that it is not possible to level out the requirements more evenly than these figures indicate, but that is a situation which results from the program of purchases that the company has entered into. This was the only way in which arrangements could be made for delivery of the new planes with which they are equipping their major lines.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: I will not put in a rhetorical way but rather in a general way. Can the minister say he is satisfied that one can take a fairly optimistic view about the financial position of these two government enterprises in the next, say, five or ten years?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, perhaps I should have said, in enlargement of my answer to the hon. member's previous question and observations, that I gave intensive personal study to this very point, because I do not need to disguise my concern over the very heavy volume of capital expenditure by Trans-Canada Air Lines in the year 1960. I would have been much happier in relation to other responsibilities that the government must meet if the capital expenditure of Trans-Canada Air Lines could have been spread out more. But there was no possibility of meeting this situation in any

other way because the contracts had been entered into, deliveries are provided for in 1960, and payment must be made in this coming year.
Now as to the longer outlook, here again, Mr. Chairman, I do not propose to substitute myself for the officials of Trans-Canada Air Lines who came before the committee and were there available to be questioned on these very matters. I can only say that from the government's point of view the same due regard will be had for seeking a sound approach to the provision which must be made for these crown corporations to enable them to discharge the function that parliament has given them to perform.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the minister made no comment after the last remarks I addressed to him. I indicated this morning that there were several stages of scrutiny of requirements. The president of the C.N.R. indicated to us that his field people thought that this year they would need capital expenditures of $272 million; that this was reviewed by a committee at head office and was brought down to $225 million; that the president himself gave it his personal attention and it was brought down to $197.6 million. There is no indication here that anything happens after that comes to the government. Is that the impression the minister wants this committee to retain?
I indicated to him a place where the committee was informed that certain funds might not be necessary for this year, that if conditions were not very good some 40-odd diesel locomotives might not be required. In the interval of two months since that evidence was given to parliamentarians, does the minister want to convey the impression to this committee that the cabinet does not inquire into these things and that they sort of automatically rubber stamp a request of this kind from the crown corporation?
During the luncheon recess I made some calculations about funded debt, to which I made reference this morning, and I found that the grand total at the end of 1951, before the reorganization, amounted to $1,472 million. There was a writing off, as all people know, of some of the debt of the road, with the result that the balance sheet showed that at the end of 1952 the grand total, instead of being $1,472 million, was written down to $605 million. The total has now gone from that figure of $605 million to a total at the end of 1959 of $1,686 million. That is an increase of $1,081 million, and takes no account of an additional increase in debt that is paying no interest, namely the purchase of preferred shares.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
The original amount of purchase as shown in the balance sheet for the first year after reorganization, December 31, 1952, indicated that the preferred 4 per cent shares amounted to $754 million. In the annual report for last year they are shown as amounting to $904 million. That is an increase of $150 million, in addition to the $1,081 million which I have indicated as the amount of increase in funded debt since reorganization. In other words, it shows a total increase since December 31, 1952 of $1,231 million. I am not saying that has not progressed under the former administration as well as the present, but I do say that there were at least three surpluses during the previous regime and we have not had them recently.
The hon. member for Port Arthur raised some very pertinent questions today, as to whether this supply of new funds year by year has actually improved the financial position of the road. I think all of us in the committee would be perturbed if we felt that the minister and his colleagues simply felt obligated to approve automatically a request which came from the management when we are dealing with outstanding sums such as we have been talking about today.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, to anyone who has not been following this debate, the hon. member's remarks would leave a very misleading impression. I dealt with this subject before the luncheon adjournment, and I made it quite clear that the capital budget of Canadian National Railways, like the capital budgets of other crown corporation, comes before the government. It is reviewed in the Department of Finance before it is approved. The hon. member, I am sure, must be familiar with the law in that regard.
I do not know of any justification that anybody has had for suggesting that the government has operated in any respect like a rubber stamp. I have never heard that allegation asserted before, Mr. Chairman, in relation to the discharge of the responsibilities of the Department of Finance in reviewing budgets and expenditures.
What the hon. gentleman had to say earlier on the subject of equipment acquisition also called for some comment. When any large corporation of this kind prepares its program of capital investment it is not possible to fit it wholly into the groove of the measurement of the 365 days of the year that the calendar creates. These are plans which naturally require time to fulfil. Questions arise as to forward commitments, as to deliveries, and many other things which affect the tempo and rate of the acquisition of equipment and
Canadian National Railways the fulfilment of programs of capital investment. The C.N.R. has done what any corporation would do in its planning in this respect. It has a requirement in relation to capital equipment and it makes the best estimate as to what, in the first place, it is prudent to acquire within the succeeding calendar year from a financial point of view. Within that limit, again, is the question of what may be expected in the way of deliveries.
That is the situation in which we find ourselves with respect to this matter of equipment. Full disclosure was made in the committee as to the equipment requirements and the plans of the company for the acquisition of equipment, including the diesels. The corporation has based its budget upon deliveries of some of the capital equipment needs that it projected. I think this is all on record before the committee.

Is the minister, in effect, saying to all of us that notwithstanding the statement which I read from page 55 of the committee report, made over two months ago by the president of the railroad, that 40 locomotive units might not be required if economic conditions were not good-is the minister saying that despite this he does not propose, between this stage of the debate and his presentation of a bill in which he must set out certain figures, to make any inquiry so we can be sure when we are asked to pass a bill with certain sums of money mentioned in it that these are the minimum sums which will be required for 1960?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I hope the hon. gentleman is not going to persist in trying to put words in my mouth which were never there. He has been at pains to take certain capital expenditures proposed for 1960 and try to relate those expenditures to 40 diesel locomotives. The fact is that in the equipment classification plans of the C.N.R. there are not 40 locomotives contemplated, but 140. There is other equipment which the company plans to acquire, and the information which the company has furnished indicates that this sum which is provided for here in relation to capital equipment, totalling approximately $35 million, is what is going to be required in 1960 and will need to be paid for in 1960. That is the item amounting to $35 million in round figures. That is the request by the company for the acquisition of equipment. It is related to a need for a substantial volume of equipment, and it will be acquired as available in 1960.

Whether or not this equipment is secured in 1960, or paid for in 1960, is the minister going to say to this committee

Canadian National Railways that in the bill he is to present based on the present resolution there will not be included an authorization to the C.N.R. to make this commitment for the 40 diesels I mention at a future date, or that there is not still an opportunity to cancel this decision in view of present economic considerations?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know what present economic considerations the hon. gentleman has in mind.
The operating results of the railroad.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman has been attempting today to rewrite the current budget of the C.N.R., and to paint a gloomy picture as to the prospects of the company. 1 have said in reply that I do not intend, and I do not think it is my function, to stand here and revise the estimates which were put forward by the competent management of the C.N.R.
In relation to the acquisition of equipment in the capital investment program of the company for this year what is provided for here is the acquisition of a portion of a much larger total of locomotives, passenger cars, freight cars and work equipment units. The company has asked for a sum of approximately $35 million designed to make provision for what is considered a reasonable portion of this capital equipment need; reasonable from the standpoint of the resources available to meet it, and reasonable from the point of view of expectation of deliveries in 1960.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the resolution carry?

No. Specifically on this resolution, I ask whether these 40 diesel locomotives are not part and parcel of the phrasing of this resolution. If the resolution were passed without amendment, or without amendment in the bill, would we not be giving authority to Canadian National Railways to make certain capital expenditures or to enter into certain contracts prior to July 1, 1961 respecting these units commitments which extend for almost 13 months ahead? I am referring, of course, to the locomotives. All I have asked the minister to do is to inquire of the management of the C.N.R. before he presents his bill to this house in final form on second reading; to ask the management and report to this house whether the company intends to order these 40 diesel locomotives, because two months ago the president of the railroad said that if economic conditions were not good they probably would not be required.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If it will make the hon. gentleman any happier I will be

glad to ask the management of the C.N.R. the question he put. However, I doubt very much if it will have any effect on the figures submitted to us here today. I have talked about the figure for acquisition of equipment.
I have referred to the fact that this is a portion or fraction of a larger program for the acquisition of capital equipment, the aggregate of which is, in round figures, $35 million, of which $26,345,000 is related to the acquisition of locomotives, passenger cars, freight cars and work equipment units.
I should just like to add on this subject that there is no new commitment authority for diesels in this capital budget. The provision for equipment authority is all old. It has already been provided by parliament. The total of these previous commitment authorities is $33.5 million. Of this, only $20.7 million is expected to be a cash requirement this year. The rest, namely $12.8 million, will be required in the future if all the equipment is in fact ordered, and commitment authority for this purpose already exists. A large part of these sums is due to diesels.

I wonder whether the minister is able to inform the committee as to the rate of interest which Canadian National Railways must pay the government of Canada for the $400,000 which he indicated was owing to the government until very recently.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is at the current rate charged to crown corporations. As the hon. member, I think, is aware, a rate is struck every six months for the six months commencing April 1 and the six months commencing October 1. That is applicable to borrowings from the treasury by all crown corporations. It consists of the current rate that the government must pay on the sums it borrows plus a service charge of one eighth of one per cent.
Can the minister indicate what rate prevailed on the $400 million he indicated was owing?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That was owing when we came into office in June of 1957?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would have to look back for that, Mr. Chairman. The rate might very well vary from the rate set at the time the loan was entered into. That $400 million was the total of loans going back over a period of some two and a half to three years, as I recall it. The rate in each case would be set at the time the advance was made. I would have to go back and obtain the hon. member those figures.

Thank you. In his budget address on March 31 last, as reported at page 2674 of Hansard, the Minister of Finance said:
Over and above these expenditures that are charged to the budgetary accounts we have under authority of parliament disbursed considerable sums for loans, advances and a number of other essential purposes. These included loans of $325 million to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, $233 million to the C.N.R.-which, however, repaid $489 million on account of these and earlier loans from the proceeds of public issues of government guaranteed C.N.R. bonds-
I remind the minister that the C.N.R., either on its own volition or on orders from the minister, obtained $300 million, the proceeds of which loan were used to repay to the government money that had been advanced by it to the C.N.R. They offered $200 million of five year bonds at 5J per cent and $100 million of 25 year bonds at 5f per cent. I understand that the yield on the bonds offered was close to 6 per cent.
In other words the minister insisted on repayment of the advances made and on which the C.N.R. had to pay an additional burden through interest. I do not know the rate, nor does the minister offhand, but knowing interest rates as they were a number of years ago I expect that the C.N.R. paid the minister on this sum somewhere between 3 per cent and 4 per cent. The minister, because of his own financial predicament, caused the C.N.R. to apply to the money market for $300 million, and to repay with that money the advances it had received. Therefore the railway was burdened with an additional interest levied on the money obtained, and all of this merely to relieve the minister of the financial difficulties in which he found himself.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is utterly untrue.

If the minister can offer another opinion we would be interested in hearing it. He admits that the proceeds were turned over to the consolidated revenue fund in the repayment of advances. The minister will have to admit that the C.N.R. had to assume an additional interest burden because of the financial difficulties the minister was in at the time. The minister did not appeal to the money market or issue bonds. The hon. gentleman issued treasury bills-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Why do you not
inform yourself on the facts once in a while and stick to them?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order. Do we have to sit and listen to the rules of the house being broken in this way through the hon. member making observations of this kind? speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It was Paul who was beside himself.

I notice that the minister is very touchy. Before one o'clock he referred to himself as the evil minister. I know the minister as an individual is most benevolent. I am willing to grant that he is the kindest man in the committee. In my opinion the policies the minister implements are evil, and I was discussing his administration of those policies. On March 31 last as reported at page 2681 of Hansard the minister said:
During^ 1960-61 we shall probably require about $290 million for housing loans, including new and existing commitments, about $150 million for C.N.R. and T.C.A. capital investment and refunding_
On March 31 the minister indicated that he needed $150 million. Today in this resolution he indicates that he needs over $200 million. What has happened in the interval? Roughly only 70 days have elapsed, yet already there has been an increase from the announced figure of $150 million to over $200 million. How does the minister account for the discrepancy? I think the minister will agree- he will have to agree-that he asked the Canadian National Railways to pay into the consolidated revenue fund hundreds of millions of dollars which the company had to obtain from the money market at a much

Canadian National Railways higher rate of interest than the rate of interest it was obligated to pay under the terms of the advances as they were made. The minister by his own action, therefore, added an undue burden to the operating expenses of our Canadian National Railways.
At the same time I should like to reply to what I consider to be most unwarranted attacks on the Canadian National Railways, which were launched by the hon. member for Vancouver South and endorsed in some measure by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway and also the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond.
The hon. member for Vancouver South indicated that the Canadian National Railways ought to be operated on the same basis as the Canadian Pacific railway; it ought to get itself in the black, he said, and it ought to remain there. The hon. member for Vancouver South ought to realize that Canadian National Railways, when it was originally organized as a government owned enterprise, had to absorb all kinds of bankrupt railway corporations and ensure that the investors in those organizations would not lose a nickel on their investment. Therefore there was an undue burden placed on the Canadian National Railways at that time which was partially eliminated by legislation a number of years ago but has never been entirely eliminated. In addition, Canadian National Railways as a public enterprise is repeatedly called upon to serve public interest, the national interest, regardless of the balance of expenditures and revenues; whereas the Canadian Pacific Railway Company does no such thing; it is under no obligations. It operates only when there is money to be made; whereas Canadian National Railways has to operate whatever railways are needed regardless of the possibility of earning a net return. Also, Canadian National Railways has not the heritage that the Canadian Pacific railway has, in that it did not receive those vast natural resources. There is no Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company to which Canadian National Railways can appeal for other revenue to help its over-all balance account.

Will the hon. member please look at the Canadian Pacific statement and compare other railway operating revenues and leave those ancillary operations out of the picture. Also will the hon. member please remember that both railways report to the board of transport commissioners.
I will do as the hon. member asks but I will contend that Canadian National Railways have to offer many services to the Canadian people as a whole-
Such as what?
-in the national interest, which the Canadian Pacific railway will not offer.
Such as what?

The hon. member asks "Such as what?" I contend that in the matter of grain movements which, as the hon. member knows, have to be operated at a loss, Canadian National Railways is the railway which has to bear the brunt of moving grain at an uneconomical rate and the Canadian Pacific railway is able to get off relatively scot free on that account.
Will the hon. member specify?

The hon. member has only
to look at the railway map and he will immediately realize that it is Canadian National Railways that hauls the bulk of the grain out of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, and the Canadian Pacific railway has very little of this burden.

speechtext: How ridiculous.
How little you know about grain hauling.

I know a little about the
railways. I know Canadian National Railways has to bear the brunt of this uneconomical operation. I ask the hon. member to
have one look only at the railway map of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta.
I am not interested in the railway map; I am interested in getting figures to make a comparison of what the hon. member says is a fact.
I shall return to the hon. member in a moment.
What is the relative mileage of the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National in the largest grain-growing parts of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta?
He does not know anything about it.
I am not a railway director. If the hon. member knows the figures I will be very happy to have him place them on the record.
Look at the map.

I dare any hon. member on the government side of the house to produce the figures as to the mileage of each of the railway companies in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, and I think if they do they will realize that Canadian National Railways is at a distinct disadvantage.
The hon. member for Vancouver South indicated that the board of directors of the Canadian National Railways had no control over Canadian National Railways; that the control they have does not come anywhere near the authority exercised by the board of directors of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. I hope I have not misinterpreted his basic assumption in this regard. If the hon. member would take the time to investigate all the other responsibilities and offices held by the directors of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company I think he would immediately agree that these men-I believe he indicated they were 24 in number-are so occupied with so many other enterprises that they are unable to give the close supervision to the operations of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company that he and I would like to see them exercise. These are honorary positions and management has almost complete sway in this as well as in many other corporations. The hon. members for Vancouver-Kingsway and Burnaby-Richmond seem to be very concerned about Canadian National Railways being able to buy out competing truck lines. I did not hear them voice any opposition to the Canadian Pacific railway buying out truck lines.

speechtext:
At its last annual meeting the board of governors of the international bank for reconstruction and development unanimously requested the executive directors of the bank to formulate articles
4626	HOUSE OF
International Development Association of agreement of an international development association. The purpose of the resolution now before the house is to obtain the approval by parliament of the articles of agreement which have been drafted in accordance with the board's resolution to authorize participation by Canada in the association, and to authorize the payment to the association of the subscription allotted to Canada under the articles of agreement.
The articles of agreement of the association are attached as a schedule to the bill. They are to a large extent self-explanatory and for that reason it may accord with the wishes of the hon. members to reserve their remarks principally for the debate on the second reading of the bill. However, I should review, now, the main features of these articles.
The purposes of the association are to promote economic development, increase productivity and raise standards of living in the less developed areas covered by the association's membership. As hon. members know, the need of less developed countries for capital from abroad is in excess of their capacity to make payments of principal and interest on loans secured on conventional terms. The association will provide finances to meet important developmental needs on terms which are more flexible and bear less heavily on the balance of payments than those of conventional loans. It will thus help to fill an important gap in the existing international machinery for assisting less developed countries.
It is expected that the membership of the association will be the same as that of the bank. Total subscriptions will amount to $1 billion payable in five annual instalments. The subscription assigned to each prospective member will be found in schedule A to the articles of agreement. It will be seen that the more economically advanced countries, those listed in part I of the schedule, which includes Canada, will subscribe $763.07 million. Their subscriptions will be payable in gold or freely convertible currency. The less developed countries, those listed in part II of the schedule, will subscribe $236.93 million of which 10 per cent will be payable in gold or freely convertible currency, and the balance in local currency. The finances provided by the association will be used for further development in the less developed areas of the world covered by the membership of the association.
The scale of subscriptions is the same as the one used by the international bank. Under this scale, Canada's share of total subscriptions will amount to $37.83 million (U.S.) of which


approximately $8.7 million would be payable 30 days after the association started its operation and $7.3 million in each of the next four years. The articles of agreement do not involve any commitment on the part of member governments to make further contributions to the association after their initial subscriptions have been paid at the end of the four-year period. The bill now before the house limits the Canadian commitment to $37.83 million (U.S.). However, the association may at some later date review the adequacy of its resources and, if it deems desirable, authorize a general increase in subscriptions. If this were to happen and the government wished to increase the Canadian subscription, it would be necessary to seek authority from parliament.
The articles of agreement authorize the association to accept supplementary contributions in a currency other than the currency of the country making the supplementary contribution. Thus a country holding counterpart funds in another country may offer to put these funds at the disposal of the association. In considering such offers, the association will pay due regard to the possibility of effectively using the supplementary contributions and to their possible inflationary and other undesirable effects.
The association will be set up as an affiliate of the international bank and its operations will be closely integrated with those of the bank. The president of the bank is to be president of the association; both organizations are to have the same board of directors; and, to the extent possible, the staff of the bank is to be appointed to serve concurrently as the staff of the association. The close integration of the bank and the association should help to keep administrative costs down, allow the association to benefit from the accumulated experience, wisdom and knowledge of the bank, and ensure that the efficient administration and effective use of resources, which have been apparent in the operations of the bank, will also characterize the operations of the association.
The association will give assistance only to less developed areas and only to its own members. Aid to be financed from subscriptions now proposed-that is to say, from the $1 billion to be subscribed in the first five years-will all be provided in the form of loans. The terms under which the loans will be extended are not specified in the articles. They might take various forms. For example, payment of interest, or principal or both might be in a local currency; or the interest rate might be below current commercial rates; or there might be a long period of grace before payment of principal begins.

The terms of each loan will be decided by the board of directors in the light of all relevant factors.
The articles of agreement also provide that in the procurement of goods and services required for projects which it is financing the association shall give due regard to considerations of competitive international trade. The association will seek to subject the procurement of goods and services to the maximum amount of international competition and whenever possible to international competitive bidding. Firms from all member countries, including Canadian firms, will thus have the opportunity to provide the goods and services to be financed by the association.
The association will not commence operations before September 15, 1960 and the articles of agreement will remain open for signature until December 31, 1960. The agreement will not come into force until it has been signed on behalf of the governments whose subscriptions comprise not less than 65 per cent of total subscriptions. Many of the main potential contributors have already initiated the legislative action necessary to allow them to become members of the association. In the United States the Senate has already approved the legislation; the banking and currency committee of the House of Representatives has also approved it and the legislation is expected to go before the house some time this week. In the United Kingdom I understand from our latest information that the second and third readings of the bill have been completed in the House of Commons and the second reading in the House of Lords. In Australia the legislation has received royal assent. In other countries, such as Germany, France and Norway, legislative action has also been taken.
The proposal to establish the international development association has received widespread support. All major industrial countries have indicated their willingness to subscribe to the association. The administrative and operational arrangements provided for in the articles of agreement will, I believe, ensure the efficient management and operation of the association.
Hon. members will, I am sure, agree that it is in Canada's general political and economic interest to assist less developed countries in their efforts to accelerate the pace of their economic development. The establishment of the international development association will add substantially to the flow of assistance already going to these countries and will provide this assistance on terms and conditions which are not presently available from any existing international organization and which are well suited to meet the needs of less developed countries.

speechtext:
Our group very definitely intends to support this resolution. We believe that the more we can do in the matter of supplying help to and the capital needs of underdeveloped nations the better. We believe that it is not only our moral duty to do this but that it is in our own national long term economic interest to help underdeveloped countries of the world to raise their standards of living because in our opinion this will add to the potential markets available to Canadian export interests.
I should like to make one proposition. It is now being proposed that we establish yet another international organization in order to make capital funds available to help the development of the underdeveloped areas of the world. I am a little afraid that there may be duplication of effort and endless expense in overhead. I would much rather have noted an attempt to expand existing organizations so that this particular need might be met.
We have the international bank, we have the International Finance Corporation, we have the Colombo plan, we have the various agencies under the auspices of the United Nations. Now it is being proposed that yet another international agency be created for what is basically the same purpose as is the purpose of a variety of existing organizations. I believe that we are getting overloaded with numbers of agencies and that we might more usefully have explored the possibilities of amending the legislation having to do with existing organizations in order that we might accomplish the aims of the organization that it is now proposed we affiliate ourselves with.
I am a keen observer of the investments being made by Canada and by Canadians in other nations and investments being made by outside agencies in Canada. If we are really 79951-0-292i

International Development Association concerned with the brotherhood of man and with the development or the maintenance of world peace I think all of us ought to be concerned with the realization that for a goodly number of years now we have been on balance importers of investment capital. I believe this is wrong. I believe that when we consider the world as one community we in Canada ought to be a little ashamed of what has happened. I believe that on balance we ought to be exporters of capital rather than importers.
I appreciate this resolution because it will help a little bit toward what I feel is the over-all aim that the rich ought to help those who are less rich and that Canada has a responsibility to the rest of the world community. My only reservation is as to the method being offered. I feel that we might very well have used other facilities of the United Nations, and that would be most preferable. However, if that was impossible of accomplishment we might have extended either the international bank or the Colombo plan in order to meet the aims that are now offered.
We heard only a little while ago that the government is giving very serious consideration to even yet another international organization in order to help the nations of Africa. I regret that the line of development is in the direction of more and more independent organizations. I believe that in the interests of economy and efficiency we ought to pay a lot more attention than we have in the past to this. Rather than entertaining each and every new brain wave that appears on the international scene we ought to consider the lack of mobility of existing organizations with the aim that we might expand those organizations to accomplish our larger aim.

International Development Association
This international development association seeks to assist, as I followed the minister and from the researches that I have been able to make, the underdeveloped countries or, as they are more correctly called, the less-developed countries of the free world by extending the flow of developmental capital on terms which are more flexible than those which exist now under any existing agency.
I share some of the concerns of the hon. member who has just spoken about the increasing establishment of international organizations. I was concerned as to why the objects of this particular body could not have been served by some modification in the international bank for reconstruction and development. I am satisfied why that is not possible. I have before me the special report of the national advisory council in the United States on the proposed international development association. It is therein pointed out that the international bank for reconstruction and development, which has made such a notable contribution, now finances its operations almost entirely by borrowing in open capital markets.
As we know, the bond issues of the international bank are made available to private investors in all countries which are members and perhaps, for that matter, in the markets of the world, and I think 75 per cent of the debentures are supported and guaranteed by what I would call the donor countries. The report goes on to say on page 1:
Accordingly, its loans must carry rates of interest sufficient to cover the bank's own interest and administrative cost and to provide reserves against the possibility of default. The term of its loans must be related, though less directly, to the maturity at which the bank itself borrows. It must receive payment in the currencies lent. The bank cannot prudently lend unless there is the probability that borrowers can service loans on the terms required by the conditions of the bank's operations.
I think that is an explanation as to why the bank, certainly as now constituted, could not provide this service although, as the Minister of Finance said, this new association is to be regarded hereafter as an affiliate of the international bank. I think the need for this particular fund must be apparent to anyone who has any appreciation of the condition of the underdeveloped countries of the world, whether they be in Asia, Latin America, Africa or the Middle East. We are not going to have peace unless the more fortunate nations recognize their obligations toward these less developed countries. That is the philosophy and motivation of this proposal.
All countries need capital for their growth. Those countries with low savings and low


income present the greatest need for capital assistance. I have mentioned some of the regions. The less developed countries need large amounts of capital. They need large amounts of capital equipment to encourage and to realize the development that is required. All we have to do is to remember the effectiveness of the Marshall plan in Europe which set into being the productive processes of the economic system in Europe. The new prosperity of Europe may be largely attributed to the assistance given by the Marshall plan and in essence, in principle, this particular proposal is designed for the same purpose in the less developed areas.
These less developed countries, as I say, need capital just as we all do. Some of this capital they can get out of their own current savings. Some can be obtained by them by borrowing in conventional ways and some capital can be obtained by assistance from private investors. But in most of these less developed countries the need for capital imports is in excess of the amounts which they can hope to secure through the regular channels I have just mentioned, so the justification of this multilateral body must be apparent to all members.
I have examined the articles of agreement with some thoroughness. It is interesting to note that the number of countries that will be on the receiving end and who are listed in part II of the schedule is considerable. As the minister pointed out, their total contributions to the $1 billion fund will be $236,930,000 compared with contributions amounting to $763,007,000 which are to be provided by those countries in part I, which includes Canada and, of course, most of the countries in the western world as well as Australia and Japan.
I note with interest that while the United States will be the largest contributor and the United Kingdom next, followed by Germany and France, Canada will be the fifth largest contributor in this group. Our subscription, which is provided for in the resolution, is to be $37,830,000 payable, as the minister observed, over a period of five years. That, by the way, provides a flexibility which should encourage many other countries to join the association, an encouragement that is not open in the case of some other organizations such as the Colombo plan and even the technical assistance operations of the United Nations.
The United States contribution is to be $320,290,000 and the other so-called economically strong countries are to provide $442,780,000. An interesting feature of the articles of agreement is that the funds provided

by all the countries, both those which will be entirely in the lender class, as it were, and those which will be in the class of both lenders and beneficiaries, are to be freely convertible. That has, of course, positive advantages but, as the hon. member for Welland pointed out a few minutes ago, it has for Canada some potential dangers which the minister feels have already been anticipated by the wording of the articles of agreement. However, I do want to say a word about this danger for Canada.
The developing countries are themselves to subscribe $236,930,000 and I understand from reading the articles of agreement that 10 per cent of this amount will be freely convertible. The subscriptions are to be paid as I said, over a five-year period and the contributions by the less developed countries are only circumscribed by the examination of each project as it will be presented. However, there is a statement in the words of approval given the whole plan by the President of the United States that I think should be examined. I look at section 2 (a) of article III of the agreement and I find that it reads this way. Even though the section is long I read it because of its importance to Canada. It is in these words:
The association may enter into arrangements, on such terms and conditions consistent with the provisions of this agreement as may be agreed upon, to receive from any member, in addition to the amounts payable by such member on account of its initial or any additional subscription, supplementary resources in the currency of another member, provided that the association shall not enter into any such arrangement unless the association is satisfied that the member whose currency is involved agrees to the use of such currency as supplementary resources and to the terms and conditions governing such use.
Now this feature of convertibility is unique. It is certainly one of the reasons why the resources of or the institution of the bank itself could not be used. I have no doubt that the government of the United States and other signatories to these articles of agreement intend to give the interpretation which the Minister of Finance says this particular section warrants. However, I notice that in the letter of transmittal by the President of the United States to congress he says, in the middle section of his letter, the following:
In addition, the association may accept supplementary resources provided by one member in the currency of another member. Thus, some part of the foreign currencies acquired by the United States primarily from its sales of surplus agricultural commodities may be made available to the association when desirable and agreed to by the member whose currency is involved.
Now there have been stories in some financial journals recently indicating, because of
International Development Association the growing surpluses of agricultural products in the United States, that some of the concerns which the people of that country feel towards future methods for the disposal of those surpluses. We should be alerted to this potential situation. I would suggest to the Minister of Finance that Canada ought to give very careful consideration to whether the United States fully subscribes to the minister's understanding of what section 2 has to say in that regard. The two sentences I have read from the President's letter of transmittal, certainly warrant the suggestion that this matter should be looked at carefully.
The minister has said he is going to suggest that this matter be sent to the committee on banking and commerce. That is a wise suggestion. It will afford an opportunity of examining the articles of agreement in detail and learning about those articles from Mr. Rasminsky. I fully subscribe to the deserved tribute which the Minister of Finance has paid to Mr. Rasminsky whose services were noted by the minister as extending from 1945. Of course Mr. Rasminsky served Canada long before that in the bank. He served in the economic section of the League of Nations over a long period. He was one of the most constructive officials at Bretton Woods, as the minister noted. He is one of those men who will be enshrined in history because of his work in connection with the establishment of the economic and social council of the United Nations.
And so this concept does provide an opportunity for countries like our own to promote conditions of peace in the world. This is one of the most effective ways by which that can be done. It is only fair when we criticize the United States so much in this house, I think generally with justification, that we should observe that the idea for this further assistance came from that country, a country that has been most generous with its resources and with its treasure in trying to assist areas of the world that need assistance, particularly since the end of the second world war. It is perhaps symptomatic of the tensions that prevail and the clashes that exist between the two main ideological divisions that the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics is not designated here as a potential member. It is interesting to note, however, that such countries as the United Arab Republic and Israel are included in part II, as well, of course, as countries like Australia, Belgium and the great powers and Japan, in part I. This particular resolution, Mr. Chairman, is one which will receive wide support in this house, in principle, and I believe that in the effort that civilized countries are making today to achieve peace this venture will,

The principle of this resolution is one which all hon. members can support. It is a principle which recognizes a duty and obligation on the part of those countries which have developed a fairly high standard of living to assist with the development of those countries which are developed to a lesser extent. The legislation to follow this resolution, as the minister pointed out, will enable Canada to make her contribution, thus encouraging development, increasing productivity and raising the standards of living in underdeveloped countries. This is a very worthy motive. It is inspiring when the have nations of the world can engage in a co-operative effort of this kind to assist the have not nations.
However, if the principle is good with respect to other countries of the world, surely the principle is equally good in its application to the underdeveloped parts of our own country. What a great thing it would be for the unity of Canada if the more developed provinces, the richer provinces of Canada, would engage in a similar co-operative effort to assist in the development of those parts of our country which are still underdeveloped. Is it too much to hope that before long the minister will introduce legislation embodying the very same principle to set up some development corporation or some fund that will be used in a similar way for the development of other parts of our own country.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ABSENTEE PAYMENTS, RESIDENCE QUALIFICATIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before the resolution carries I should like to make a short statement with reference to the proposed bill.
The War Veterans Allowance Act has provided for some 30 years financial assistance to many veterans and widows of veterans. The act was designed to alleviate the difficult conditions which many older veterans
War Veterans Allowance Act and their families had to face because of limited income and resources, particularly where their problems were complicated by impaired health or advancing years. The act has been reviewed on a number of occasions and has been amended from time to time to meet changing conditions. At the present time it is providing assistance to some 68,000 veterans and widows.
One of the provisions which has applied since the beginning has been the requirement that a recipient of an allowance must be residing in Canada in order to receive it. Some years ago the principle was modified slightly by permitting recipients to absent themselves for limited periods and receive on their return, provided they were still qualified, the payment of the allowance for their period of absence. This period was increased three years ago to permit an absence of six months after which they would be eligible to receive the allowance upon their return to Canada.
It has become apparent that for various reasons a number of veterans and widows who have qualified for the allowance while in Canada would find it desirable to reside outside this country for longer periods. The persons of whom I am thinking are those who have fully qualified for an allowance and have been recipients for some time in this country. Instances have come to our attention where some recipients' health would be improved if they were able to take up residence in climates less severe than that which they are likely to encounter in this country. There are other instances where families have dispersed and the call of family ties would encourage them to live with or near members of the family who are unable to return or move to Canada.
The government has been concerned about these veterans and widows and has felt that this was an opportune time in which to take steps to permit the continuance of an allowance to a recipient who would find it desirable to absent himself from Canada for an indefinite period. A similar principle is being considered with relation to the Old Age Security Act where the government has also felt some freedom should be granted to pensioners under that act to change their residence to other countries.
The proposed amendments contained in the bill are not intended to reflect the results of a thorough review of this legislation such as the one we made in 1957, but to incorporate at this time the principle of flexibility of residence which I have explained. One of the conditions involved is that in order to be eligible for an allowance outside of this country a recipient must have resided continuously in Canada for 12 months before

War Veterans Allowance Act he absents himself. I think this is a desirable provision because it establishes the principle that veterans and widows who wish to have the allowance paid to them outside of Canada must in effect be bona fide Canadian residents and thus be persons for whom the allowance was originally intended.
It has not been possible to estimate how many veterans or widows who are recipients under the act will absent themselves from Canada and will continue to receive the allowance. There will be administrative problems introduced by the payment of allowances outside this country because, as I mentioned, the allowance is payable only where recipients are in necessitous circumstances. The war veterans allowance board are working out the necessary administrative arrangements to provide that the principle of the means test will be adequately maintained. Each recipient who absents himself will be acquainted with all matters relating to the continuance of payment outside of Canada so that there will be no misapprehension on the part of any recipient.
There is one other amendment to the act which is proposed by the bill. When the act was last amended during the 1957-58 session one of the amendments reduced from 20 years to 10 years the Canadian residence requirement for eligibility for an allowance for a former member of His Majesty's forces or the forces of His Majesty's allies or associated powers where the qualifying service was in any war concluded on or before August 31, 1921. It now seems desirable to establish a corresponding Canadian residence qualification for former members of His Majesty's forces or allies who served during world war II, thus allowing treatment of these veterans on a basis similar to that now available to the veterans of His Majesty's forces or allies who served in earlier wars. The number of veterans who will qualify for an allowance on this basis is not great, but I think hon. members will agree that they should not be deprived of an eligibility which their comrades of earlier wars now have.
Mr. Chairman, as has become customary with all bills respecting amendments to the acts contained in the veterans charter, I anticipate that this bill following second reading will be referred to the standing committee on veterans affairs where it will be thoroughly reviewed by the committee members who are well acquainted with the present provisions of the act. It will afford an opportunity for a detailed explanation of the clauses of this bill and I am sure that it will be thoroughly studied.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to indicate our support for this resolution,

which I am sure will also have the support of every hon. member of the committee. This resolution envisages an amendment to the War Veterans Allowance Act which in many respects is the counterpart of an amendment which was passed recently with respect to the Old Age Security Act. Just as the amendment to the Old Age Security Act will enable old age pensioners to receive their pensions when living abroad so will the amendment implied in this resolution permit war veterans under certain conditions to receive their war veterans allowance while living outside of Canada. This is a principle which every hon. member of the committee will heartily endorse.
We recognize that this measure is necessary because many veterans, as the minister has just pointed out, for health reasons alone are compelled to live outside of Canada in a climate more conducive to a state of good health. There are also many lonely veterans who would like to spend months and perhaps even years visiting their various relatives who live in different parts of the world. Formerly they could do this only by forfeiting their war veterans allowance or by returning after a certain period in order to reinstate themselves. Therefore the amendment involved in this resolution will be of great convenience to these people.
While this legislation envisaged in this resolution does parallel the amendment to the Old Age Security Act, it is different in one very important respect. The old age pensioner receives his pension as a matter of right. The veteran receives his war veterans allowance not as a matter of right but in conformity with a means test. This, as the minister has said, will involve some administrative problems and for that reason we welcome his statement that the legislation will be referred to the standing committee on veterans affairs. There it could be thoroughly reviewed, and every aspect of this application could be thoroughly discussed. No doubt there would be some very useful suggestions, as always, from this committee for the improvement of the original bill. At this stage we are concerned only with the principle of the resolution, and I give it my hearty support.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ABSENTEE PAYMENTS, RESIDENCE QUALIFICATIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
I have sat here all day anticipating this resolution coming before the committee. Then I was unavoidably detained and had to rush down on being telephoned by the hon. member for Vancouver East. Anyway, as usual, I have arrived.
I must say I rise to support the principle and purpose of this legislation on behalf of this group. This bill will not affect a large number of veterans or their dependents, but it will mean a great deal to those it does

affect. I first urged on behalf of this group an amendment to the War Veterans Allowance Act along these lines eight years ago, and I will tell hon. members the reason why. The need for such an amendment was brought to my attention owing to the sad case of a personal friend of mine who was a veteran living on the Arrow lakes. This veteran was a first world war veteran who had lost his son in the second world war. After he became about 65 years of age he found it necessary to apply for a war veterans allowance, and he received it after some three or four years while a resident there. He suffered from a very severe non-pensionable bronchial condition, some obscure lung trouble. He went to Shaughnessy on a number of occasions but nothing could be done for him.
Finally the Department of Veterans Affairs said the only way to prolong his life and obtain a greater measure of comfort or, perhaps I should say, a greater absence of misery, was to live at a high altitude in a dry climate. Consequently this poor veteran sold his small property for $700 and went to live in a little village near Mexico City. He soon exhausted his $700. Of course, having left Canada, he was not entitled at that time to continue to receive the war veterans allowance. After his small capital was exhausted he was maintained by a few friends who used to send him a few dollars a month where he lived in this little village near Mexico City.
Then one day I got a letter from some Mexican peasants, written by a person who could write and understand English. Apparently they had found some of my letters in his belongings. They informed me that they had picked him up; that they had found his body on the street. They knew where he lived. They had known him for the year or two during which he lived there. They had gone to his quarters and found these letters which I and other persons had written. In the letter they said, we liked this nice old veteran very much and he was a good friend of ours and we did all we could to take care of him because we knew he was very poor. But we are very poor people, too. In order to see that he got a decent funeral we collected about 700 pesos and buried him with due respect and reverence but, being poor people, we cannot afford to lose the 700 pesos. Is there any way in which you can see we get our money back?
I took the matter up with the Department of Veterans Affairs, with Mr. G. H. Parliament, the director general of welfare services and with the Department of External Affairs. The Department of External Affairs, through its officers in Mexico, arranged to
War Veterans Allowance Act repay the money to the villagers in question and thank them on behalf of the government of Canada for having taken care of this ailing veteran.
This incident brought to my attention the need for some provision whereby a veteran in receipt of war veterans allowance should be allowed to continue to receive this benefit during his absence from Canada. I believed in the principle that a person who had served this country in war was entitled to spend his declining years wherever he wished and to receive the allowance. However, I found I could not make much headway in that direction so, at the time, while supporting the principle of this bill and the purpose of this resolution, I urged the government to consider permitting a veteran to receive the allowance if he was forced to live outside Canada, particularly on the recommendation of doctors of the Department of Veterans Affairs.
I brought the matter to the attention of the house over a period of years-in 1952, 1953, 1954, 1955 and so on. Then, because of the circumstances of this particular veteran whose story became known to the veterans throughout Kootenay West, a number of legion branches-and I have a lot of very active legion branches in my constituency-took the matter up and passed a resolution urging that Canadian veterans residing outside Canada and otherwise qualified should be granted war veterans allowance. Then the matter was taken up at a dominion conference, and as a result of the expression of an opinion of the dominion conference the dominion representatives of the Legion made representations to the government and to the veterans affairs committee, first in 1953.
I just want to read the resolution they brought before the committee in 1953 in this connection. The recommendation was that Canadian veterans resident outside Canada and otherwise qualified for a grant of war veterans allowance should be entitled to receive it. The comment in connection with this resolution was as follows:
Many veterans of the Canadian forces have found it necessary for health reasons, possibly due to pensionable disability, to reside outside Canada. We feel that these veterans should not be denied the right to war veterans allowances. The numbers are small and the cost would not be great if this recommendation were acted upon.
The matter was discussed by the committee and, as the hon. minister will recall, it had sympathetic support of the committee. The Legion presented a similar resolution the following year and, later, the minister of that day, Mr. Lapointe, said he would study the question. He did so, and later reported during a discussion in this house of the estimates of his department that while

War Veterans Allowance Act he considered there was considerable merit in the suggestion he could not recommend it because of administrative difficulties. There were serious problems, he said, in that connection, and on that ground he could not recommend the suggestion to the government.
I as one of the members of this group am very pleased that this resolution has come before us, and I am sure this applies to all members of the House of Commons. As I said in my opening remarks, this will not affect a large number of veterans. It will not be a matter of great expense to the treasury of Canada. But it will be of great advantage to those whom it does affect and it will be bringing much happiness to a certain number of veterans and their dependents. It will do this for three reasons: first, and most essential, when a veteran finds it necessary to live in some other climate on account of his health. Second, owing to family circumstances-and I am sure we all know these circumstances-he finds it to his advantage and perhaps to his relatives' advantage to live in another country with them. Third, in some cases he wishes to continue a youthful friendship in his declining years and live with friends or a former associate or comrade. maintopic: CANADA-NETHERLANDS INCOME TAX AGREEMENT ACT AMENDMENT TO APPROVE SUPPLEMENTARY CONVENTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to implement the supplementary income tax convention between Canada and the Netherlands which was signed on October 28, 1959. The supplementary convention is set forth in a schedule to the bill. This supplementary convention modifies the original convention which was signed on April 2, 1957, and approved by parliament shortly thereafter. It is chapter 16 of the statutes of 1957, assented to on April 12, 1957.
This bill and the supplementary convention are in the same form as others which have been before the house, and I would refer the house particularly to the act to amend the Canada-United States Tax Convention Act, which was approved by the house in 1956.
Hon. members, of course, are well aware of the general pattern of Canada's income tax conventions with other countries. Consideration was given to the most recent of them- the Canada-Finland income tax convention- in this house only last June. It is unnecessary therefore for me to describe the terms of the original convention with the Netherlands, and it will be sufficient to give an account of the ways in which the supplementary convention modifies the original convention, which is chapter 16 of the statutes of 1957.
The proposed supplementary convention is intended to settle certain problems encountered by both countries under the terms of the original convention. There are, in fact, three changes.
The first change which hon. members will find in article 1 of paragraph (a) merely provides for the deletion from the original convention of the special provisions which permitted the speedy termination of two articles. These articles provided for a maximum rate of withholding tax on dividends and interest having their sources in one country and going to the residents of the other country. These special termination provisions were in addition to the normal provisions for terminating the convention and were inserted to enable either country to increase its withholding tax on six months' notice. In the absence of such special provisions it would have been necessary to rely on

the normal termination provisions but they could not be invoked before June 30, 1959. Now that this date of June 30 is past, there is no need to retain the special termination provision.
The second change, which is contained in article 1, paragraph (b) of the supplementary convention, concerns the rate of withholding tax applicable to dividends from a subsidiary company resident in one country to its parent company resident in the other. Under the Income Tax Act the rate on such dividends is 5 per cent if the subsidiary is wholly owned by the parent company. In many of our income tax conventions this requirement for ownership is reduced from 100 per cent to a majority of the shares; that is, the requirement is for control rather than for complete ownership. In our convention with the United Kingdom the 100 per cent ownership provision was retained but the rate of tax was reduced to zero. In the original convention with the Netherlands both the ownership requirement and the rate of tax were reduced, the ownership requirement to a majority of the shares and the rate to zero. Thus the provision in the original convention is less restrictive than in any other of the conventions into which Canada has entered.
This provision has been changed in the supplementary convention so that the requirement for ownership is 100 per cent rather than a majority of the shares and the rate of tax is 21 per cent rather than zero. This change will make it possible to collect more revenue in withholding taxes and it will bring the convention with the Netherlands into closer harmony with our other income tax conventions.
There is however-and I must point this out to the house-one exception to this principle. If the subsidiary company merely receives income in the form of dividends and interest from companies abroad and receives no income from its own country of residence the rate of tax on dividends sent abroad to its parent company will continue to be nil. But to take advantage of this concession such a company will henceforth have to be 100 per cent owned rather than merely controlled by the parent company as at present. This means that where this form of investment income is merely funnelled through a holding company in Canada and does not have its source here it will continue to be free of tax.
Then, there is a third change which is contained in article II and the effect is to prevent withholding tax from being levied on alimony from a resident of one country to a resident of the other. Alimony will thus be treated in the same way as pensions. The practical effect is that Canada will give up its

withholding tax on alimony going to residents *of the Netherlands but will not have to give a credit in respect of Netherlands tax against its income tax on a Canadian resident who receives alimony from the Netherlands, as it was formerly bound to do.

subtopic: PROVISIONS FOR CONSTRUCTION OF TERMINAL FACILITIES AT TORONTO
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this resolution seeks to authorize the Canadian National Railways to construct certain railway terminal facilities in the metropolitan Toronto area. I should like to say a few words about the nature of the improvements and expansion which are proposed, the estimates of cost, and the economic and operating features of the plan.
It is a fundamental principle of this government that in order to enable it to operate efficiently and economically, and thereby offer the greatest values to the public, the established capital needs of the publicly-owned system must be met. This government has encouraged, and proposes to give continued encouragement to capital projects that are submitted to it by the railway management that can be recognized as self-liquidating. The project which is the subject matter of the resolution is in that category.
I should like the committee to view it in relation to what is being done across the country to adjust the railway plant and services to the needs of today, raise the level of productivity and achieve economies. In this regard strong emphasis has been placed in recent years on the need to provide better yard facilities for handling trains in terminals. Yard extensions and improvements have just been or are being completed at Halifax, North Sydney, St. John's, Corner Brook, Campbellton, Joffre, Garneau, Sarnia, Edmonton and Port Mann. The plan calls for linking all these modernized facilities with electronically controlled hump yards at the four major centres of Moncton, Montreal, Toronto and Winnipeg. The work is advancing rapidly at Montreal, Moncton and Winnipeg, but the full benefits of the capital expenditures in these yards will not be realized until similar facilities have been completed at Toronto. The yard proposed for Toronto is thus an essential element of this important chain.
As hon. members will remember, Canadian National Railways was created after world war I to operate as one system various railways previously operated directly by the government, as well as those of the privately owned Grand Trunk and Canadian Northern systems. These railways, in many instances had constructed their own separate terminal facilities at various locations. The integration of these facilities has been an exhaustive

process, and is not yet finished. For instance, in the city of Toronto at the present time, no fewer than eight freight yards are operated by the Canadian National. Due to their limited capacity and the lack of available property around it is not possible to expand any one of these yards to provide the central classification facilities that are needed for the marshalling of trains in an efficient and economical manner. However, even if the proposed facilities could be located on the site of an existing yard or on existing lines there are other features that would have to be considered.
Canadian National Railways operate passenger trains, with mail and express cars, and freight trains over six separate lines or subdivisions radiating from the Toronto union station area, from the Bathurst street yard in the west to the Don yard in the east. Three lines diverge from the west end and two others from the east. The sixth has its junction about five miles east of the Don, and its traffic is also fed into the heart of the congested area. Railway traffic is thus concentrated between Bathurst street and the Don river and, to add to the congestion, there are continual cross-over movements necessitated by the fact that there are numerous facilities such as express and freight stations, team tracks, and yard and harbour facilities located on either side of the main line. The congestion causes delays and costly handling of traffic.
The management of Canadian National believes that in these circumstances the only practical, long term solution that will obviate delays and costly handling, provide more efficient service, and reduce operating costs, is to construct a modern, electronically controlled hump yard and related facilities in an entirely new location outside of the congested area. The site which has been selected is in Vaughan township, and access lines to this yard, as planned, will run from Pickering in the east and through Malton in the west, circumventing the congested Don-Bathurst street area. This is considered to be the most feasible location from the combined standpoints of engineering, operation, land use and zoning, cost and return on investment.
The gross capital requirement for this project is estimated at $37 million. The annual savings in operating expenses will be substantial, not to mention several non-assessable benefits which are expected to accrue from the construction. For one thing, the reduction in the handling time of cars will substantially improve freight deliveries. Shippers will thereby be better served and more apt to increase their railway shipments. Second, the considerable reduction in terminal delays will
Canadian National Railways increase the availability and use of road power. The fact that over-all fewer units of road power have to be used has a certain value which cannot be accurately computed, but is nevertheless appreciable, particularly during times of shortage of motive power. A third and very important benefit lies in the opening up of large new industrial areas which can be economically served by the proposed lines.
This program of construction is not designed simply to resolve local problems. It is, as I have indicated at the outset, part of a long range plan for greater efficiency and more economical operation of the railway system as a whole. Improved operating efficiency is the key to lower transportation charges, and for this reason the proposed measure is of direct interest to the public and to shippers all over Canada who have shouldered in the past the burden of freight rate increases occasioned by rising operation costs. As such it will benefit farmers in western Canada equally as well as shippers in the maritimes and in the central provinces. For all these considerations, I earnestly hope that the resolution will commend itself to all hon. members.
I might say, Mr. Chairman, that after second reading of this bill I shall move that it be referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines for examination by that committee.
