speechtext:
This evening, Mr. Chairman, I have had the advantage of being largely in agreement with respect to most of the legislation which has been before us. With this resolution, too, we of the Liberal party are in accord. The terminal, of which this legislation will permit the construction, is designed primarily, as the minister has told us, to serve the Toronto metropolitan area. As all hon. members know, this is a great industrial city which has experienced a rapid, almost explosive, growth, particularly in the last decade since the second world war. The very nature of this rapid growth has increased the problems to which the minister has referred in connection with industrial development, which had been concentrated more or less in the central areas of the city and which has now been moved, enlarged and augmented by new industry situated in the periphery of the metropolitan area from Etobicoke on the west through to North York, Scarborough and Pickering on the east. This has considerably increased the problem of handling traffic to service all of this new major and supplementary industry.
We welcome this new development which the minister has referred to this evening. It is a development of considerable magnitude,

Canadian National Railways which is witnessed by the size of the expenditure. Certainly any project involving an expenditure of the order of $100 million is one of considerable importance. It should permit the handling of freight at the north end of the city and enable this to be done more expeditiously and at the same time we hope more economically, especially to these new suburban industries I have mentioned.
The minister has said that the project will be self-liquidating. We hope this is so and also that it will bring considerable savings as he has indicated and thus reduce the cost of doing business.
There are other advantages proposed in this project. We hear a great deal about planning of our metropolitan areas these days and we have a problem in planning in Toronto, as have other great metropolitan cities. We have heard some complaint about the location of this proposed marshalling yard, but I am not qualified to speak on that. I presume the factors were carefully and sympathetically considered by the C.N.R. and by the board of transport commissioners.
This project should release the older tracks for use by commuter trains. As the minister has said, these tracks enter the downtown area of Toronto from six different avenues and they funnel into a central yard at Union station, and for years we have been talking about the possibility of an adequate commuter service to serve the downtown areas. I know that many Torontonians have looked with some envy at the excellent service enjoyed by the people of Montreal, and we hope that with this development it will be possible to use some of these facilities for a new and improved commuter service for the downtown areas.
As a matter of fact it would be possible to have quite a comprehensive rapid transit system without the expenditure of further large additional sums of money. I hope that the Toronto metro planning authorities will co-operate with the C.N.R. in trying to work out just such a comprehensive system of rapid transit, and that the two of them will work together with the Toronto transportation commission in order to avoid a duplication and to make sure there is the maximum service provided at the minimum cost.
It appears, Mr. Chairman, that this project will be beneficial to the majority of the residents of the metropolitan Toronto area, and under these circumstances I will reserve any further comment at this time until the bill is available and we have seen it.

subtopic: PROVISIONS FOR CONSTRUCTION OF TERMINAL FACILITIES AT TORONTO
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the outstanding thing about the project outlined in the

measure in front of us has been the resistance offered by certain ratepayers in the region affected by the new line. Before I review some of the points that certain groups have made I should like to indicate that I think this is a worth-while bill and I hope that the relative quiet in the last four or five months as far as this resistance is concerned indicates that everyone is happier than they were.
The main complaints of the people in the Thornhill-Markham-Vaughan areas hinge on the choice of the route of this particular Canadian National Railways by-pass line and the location of the terminal. The objections were quite extensive, but most quite naturally stemmed from self-interest and a feeling that the line and the yards were going to affect property values and the selling values of the homes and the land in the area. The complaints centred around the fact that the C.N.R. had gone ahead with the planning project as a result of a report prepared for them by De Leuw-Cather and Company and this De Leuw-Cather report was kept secret so that those who were protesting the specific location of this route were unable to determine what alternative routes there were.
Some of these ratepayer groups, such as the Thornhill-Markham-Vaughan group, tried to work out with what resources they had alternative routes. One of the points made by ratepayer associations in the Thornhill area was that the project director refused to join the ratepayers association in a study of the socio-economic effects on homes and property in the district. When asked to reveal details of the carefully concealed De Leuw-Cather report on which the project plans were supposedly based the C.N.R. refused to table it even for study by the member for the area, the hon. member for York Centre. When asked what damage would be done by a heavy traffic double track slashing through the heart of an established residential community with fine homes and schools, the C.N.R. admitted that they did not know and yet displayed no interest in helping to determine this as part of the costs involved in their route consideration.
The Toronto metro area has received very recently what you might call its "Gordon report", and it is a projection of metro's role into the year 1980. It is very interesting, if you look at the synopsis presented in either the Toronto Telegram or Star, to discover the projection for the year 1980. It is projected that the area where the yard will be will be one of the fastest growing areas in terms of population. The whole shift in population according to this metro study is northwards,

and nowhere will there be a greater concentration of population in the next 20 years than in the particular region where this yard is going to go.
The other interesting point is that the Canadian Pacific railway have plans for a marshalling yard of not quite comparable size, but of considerable size nevertheless, in the east towards Agincourt. Again if we look at the metro projection map, that is another area which will be much more heavily populated. When you look at the analysis presented in the Toronto Star of the transportation future up to the 1980's in Toronto you get this quotation which appears on page 35 of the Star for January 31, 1960:
The new C.N.R. "Toronto terminal" to be linked to its main lines by new access lines, will be one of the largest and most modern railroad terminals. The company's growing piggyback operations will be handled here.
When the new yards are completed, freight will be distributed from the outside into the city instead of from the inside out as at present. As a result, railroad facilities in the inner area will be relieved.
These facilities will still be needed to serve the industrial and commercial areas in the central part of the city and will continue to carry express, mail and interurban passengers. The report predicts this business will decrease.
The relevance of this projected yard and the tremendous growth of Toronto in the particular region around Thornhill underlines the possible conflicts and the need to be absolutely sure about the location and the plans for its extension in the future. I would hope that when we do have the bill before the committee we will have an opportunity of going into the alternative routes and be told just what consideration Canadian National Railways has in the mind of its management so far as its relationships in this area with residential development are concerned. I know the argument was put to the committee by the president of the railways that most of the objections seemed to have been circumvented and that everyone seemed to be happy with the plan. I acknowledge that I have not received any recent spate of letters on the matter such as I did last fall. But when you have a potential growth in the Toronto area and something of this size is placed into what is considered to be the largest potential there is, I think we should know what the plans of the metro planning authority will be in the matter and also where the people of Vaughan and Markham townships stand in relation to the dividing off of the area adjacent to the yards along that line for different types of industry.
It is apparent from the projection that it is expected that industry will follow the movement northward and link up with this particular railway line. It seems to me that we
Canadian National Railways could have here the makings of a really heavy congestion and also a serious conflict between the residents, the C.N.R. and potential industrial users unless we are absolutely sure that there are plans to circumvent or head off such a conflict. With the experience in our minds of the very sharp conflicts that can develop between the ratepayers in an area and Canadian National Railways, I think we should, in the committee stage, go into this matter very thoroughly. I hope the minister will agree to help persuade the committee to let us have some spokesmen from the municipality before the committee so that we can be absolutely sure that there will not be in a few years any repercussions that are going to cause difficulty for our government owned railway.

The other thing that puzzled me-and I wonder if the hon. member for Port Arthur has considered this-is that I do not recall with respect to terminal requirements at Montreal, Moncton and Winnipeg that this house was presented with anything in the nature of legislation similar to the present legislation. subtopic: PROVISIONS FOR CONSTRUCTION OF TERMINAL FACILITIES AT TORONTO
speechtext:
Rising to speak on this resolution after a rash of opposition speakers, I should like to review the background of the situation in view of the fact that the projected route which manages by one means or another to avoid any heavily populated districts as it proceeds over the north end of Toronto has landed right in the middle of one of the most beautiful areas in metropolitan Toronto.
The citizens in that area, as the hon. member for Port Arthur indicated, were disturbed and upset by the prospect of the double line -the major freight traffic line-particularly so because most of the persons resident in that area, especially in recent years, had retreated from the downtown and congested areas of Toronto with the accompanying noise and other disturbances that accompany city life and found, in more recent times, on reaching the quiet area of north Yonge street, where, somehow, were contained all the advantages of both city and country living, that the noise and disturbance had followed them

out there and were presenting a most disquieting prospect for the future of that community.
Certainly throughout the discussion which took place with respect to this matter no one took serious issue with the need for such a line; the legitimate necessity for it and the fundamental economic basis on which it was projected. The hon. member for Trinity mentioned some clash but I believe that no one quarrels with the purpose. Some relief will be provided through the projected by-pass with the spokes of the wheel, as it were, leading down to the centre of the city. The feasibility of the project for commuter traffic is demonstrated.
I do not think that anyone is too optimistic, and certainly I am not, about the ultimate prospects of commuter traffic but at least the possibility of relief exists in a more practical way. Clearly the townships in the areas adjacent to the proposed line will benefit. The establishment of the line will be welcome news to the township councils with respect to the effect this will have on balancing the municipal versus commercial tax revenues. Against that must be weighed the cost of this in terms of upset and disturbance.
I should like to commend a number of people in this connection and perhaps especially the people in the area for their vigour in pressing for action. At an earlier stage in my remarks I was going to describe Thornhill as a sleepy village but I feel that the minister, the president of the C.N.R. and anyone else who has had anything to do with the matter would probably select "sleepy" as the least appropriate word to describe the residents of the area. This group of ratepayers were most vocal in their protestations. Some were engaged in engineering and other fields. They were able to recruit from among their numbers members who were capable of making an intelligent judgment on the basis of the information that was made available to them concerning the availability of alternative proposals.
The attitude of the minister throughout has been very commendable in terms of his cooperation with me during the many interviews and discussions which we had concerning the problem. I wish I could say the same for the relationship that existed between the management of the C.N.R. and the various ratepayers' groups involved. Perhaps enough has been said about that in other quarters and what I have said will suffice. I should like the minister and the committee to know, however, that the residents of the area still feel that the explanations offered

to them in reply to the various questions they asked concerning the alternative proposals left something to be desired. This group recognized throughout the need and the essential soundness of the proposition but felt that in the handling of it and in the discussions between the crown corporation and the various citizens' groups much was left to be desired.
As far as the De Leuw-Cather report is concerned, we are concerned with a similar report of a committee of this house at this time. I am impressed by the argument that interdepartmental reports of crown corporations and government departments should not be tabled, published or become public and this particularly in a case where the C.N.R. is competing, after a fashion, with the C.P.R. However, the fact remains that in this case the information to which the ratepayers in the area felt they were entitled has not been presented to them in the form in which they required. I assume that when this matter goes to the committee some effort will be made by the minister to clear the air concerning that issue and to satisfy the residents of the area and particularly those of the village of Thornhill about the basic soundness and merits of the proposed by-pass route.
That is all I wish to say at this point. I look forward to hearing from the minister and perhaps he will comment on some of the suggestions I have made. I also look forward to further clarification when the bill reaches the committee stage.

Mr. Chairman, I am not a member of the committee that will consider this measure although I was a member of the committee that had the opportunity of examining the senior officials of the Canadian National Railways.
I know from talking outside this chamber with a number of backbench members of the Conservative party that they, too, are rather concerned about the depressing financial results of the C.N.R. I am sure that they and all other hon. members who will serve on the committee when it examines the bill that will follow this resolution will look into some of these matters very carefully.
Following the kind suggestion of the hon. member for Port Arthur I have re-read page 212 of the proceedings of the former committee which examined C.N.R. matters. I find there the phrase to which the discussion referred and the one that was always used was "Toronto by-pass matter". That is the thing the committee that will examine this new measure should examine into.
I repeat my point that we have always considered that terminal facilities would be 79951-0-293
Canadian National Railways part of the capital budget of the Canadian National Railways presented annually. Indeed, if we look at the resolution we are now considering we find that it refers to a provision for certain railway terminal facilities. My concern is this. After we had in another committee what we considered to be a proper examination of the capital expenditures of the C.N.R. as required for 1960, including expenditures relating to terminal facilities and other matters, why do we have a separate piece of legislation at this time in this respect?
Having regard to some of the discussions which we hear less formally than we usually hear in this chamber, I wonder if the members of the committee that will consider this new measure will examine carefully whether or not the competitive road is embarking on capital expenditures such as are contemplated in this resolution. Both are experiencing today rather adverse revenue records. I mentioned this morning in connection with other legislation that the operating experience of the C.N.R. for the first four months of 1960 as compared with 1959 reveal a decrease in revenue of $7.6 million. The Canadian Pacific railway-and I have the figure for three months rather than four months of 1960-reports an increase. Nobody can raise the question of dividends from subsidiaries because the revenue refers to rail income only. Their revenue was up half a million dollars. These matters should be looked at carefully when we consider further expenditures of this kind, such as were referred to this morning by the hon. member for Port Arthur when he said that these millions are being provided in a capital way but are they increasing the net revenue of our crown company?
I find also that the proposed capital expenditures involve $100 million in addition to the $197 million that we were discussing this morning, or $297 million for Canadian National Railways. I find that the Canadian Pacific proposals for 1960 are $83 million. This includes $25 million for their air subsidiary. The other figures for the C.N.R. are quite separate and apart from the Trans-Canada Air Lines, although the capital stock of the Trans-Canada Air Lines is, 1 believe, owned entirely by Canadian National Railways. I think the comparison is very striking. I am not a member of this committee but I hope it will examine very carefully some of the comparisons, such as those suggested by other hon. members earlier today.
As I say, some of those comparisons are striking and, as the hon. member for Port Arthur suggested, we have tried this for 10 years; a billion dollars has been provided in extra capital to the crown company. Are

Canadian National Railways we satisfied that these things are providing efficient operation to the extent that eventually the net income will improve sufficiently to justify the expenditures? Or, as the hon. member for Port Arthur suggested, do we as responsible representatives of the shareholders say that even if they do not provide the net revenue improvement, they are improvements to the country as a whole and are justified? But I am very disappointed to think that there would be any casualness on the part of the executive when certain paring down of demands occur at the executive level of the C.N.R., as was given in evidence with respect to their basic capital requirements, going from $272 million down to $197 million in various stages, but when it is presented to the government there is no change.
I hope that in this item as well as in the other the committee will examine the role of the executive as to prior inquiry before the legislation comes to us as a justification for capital expenditures of the magnitude that have been presented to us today.

subtopic: PROVISIONS FOR CONSTRUCTION OF TERMINAL FACILITIES AT TORONTO
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I feel it is important that this committee and the country appreciate the interest that this government has shown in the C.N.R. in recent months and during the past couple of years. Admittedly a hump yard is well under way just outside the city of Moncton. This has been a great improvement to the area and it is going to make it possible for the C.N.R. to remain competitive.
As long as the government of Canada owns the C.N.R., in my opinion there is a strong obligation on the government to give it the tools to remain competitive with other modes of transport and with the Canadian Pacific Railway. Consequently, I feel all members will agree with the principle of this legislation.
I hope the Minister of Transport will be invited to Moncton by the railway management when the hump yard in Moncton is officially opened sometime later this year. If he is invited I feel quite confident that he will attend. At the same time I suggest it would be very educational for the members from the Toronto area to accompany the minister because there they will see in operation what Toronto expects to have probably in three years time.
There has been some criticism tonight of the fact that the sessional committee did not study this particular piece of legislation. I have been on that committee for the past three years, and its major function has been to go over the policies and the previous year's operation of the C.N.R. In my opinion the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines is far more competent to study


this legislation. In the first place, the sessional committee is composed of only 16 members while the standing committee consists of 60 members representing each and every major railway and shipping area of the country. Consequently it will be possible, with management before this large standing committee, for the public and the members of parliament to understand absolutely, without any doubt, the policy of the railway management. Therefore I do not believe there is any strength or justice to the criticism that this subject should have been before the sessional committee.
Another point which I notice and which I am very pleased to see is the fact that this committee will now study the scheme before the operation goes into effect. It seems to me quite apparent that the government, or the management of the railway, has recognized the importance of letting the municipalities become familiar with the future trend and plans of this large government corporation. Too often in the past major railway decisions were made before local and municipal governments and the public of the area were notified. In this instance the people in the Toronto area will be invited to the committee and the committee will have firsthand knowledge of their thinking in so far as the proposed hump yard project is concerned.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I want to re-emphasize the fact that I am glad to see that management is going to hear and listen to the feeling of the public and I am also glad to witness that notwithstanding a series of annual deficits this government still has confidence in the railway and is stiH prepared to finance its operations.

Mr. Chairman, I am rising for the purpose of asking a question. I am a little confused as to the course of this debate for the following reason. As I understand it, we have here a resolution which is to authorize the provision of certain moneys for Canadian National Railways and the method of doing so is set out. The money is being provided for the purpose of providing certain railway works in the Toronto area. My understanding is that the railway itself, through its own officers, will negotiate with the parties in interest, the municipalities and metropolitan Toronto, if it comes in. I do not know whether it does come or not. There is also the board of transport commissioners. I ask this question. After this money is voted the matter does not concern us further, as I understand. Is it not left to those other responsible bodies to negotiate with the railway and to reach a conclusion?
I find in this debate that evidently the ideas I have in mind are very different from those of several other people who have spoken, and

they may be right. I am asking this question with this thought in mind. As I understand it, they are proposing that the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines should really go into the whole of this scheme and should make up their minds whether the Canadian National Railways is wise in entering into this scheme.
According to what I understand from some hon. members, they are going to go into all kinds of questions, questions of policy, questions of detail. It is a matter I want to raise now while we are passing this resolution so that there will not be any misunderstanding afterward. It would be very easy for the minister to explain that I am wrong and that nothing will happen, that I have simply taken up four or five minutes of the time of the committee to raise that point.
Although I was not on the committee I remember reading that a question arose as to the functions of the executive officers of the railway and apparently there was some difference of opinion as to just where those functions ended and the committee stepped in and more or less guided them. I think that is an important question. I think it is a matter of some importance to clear our minds now because if I am right then the house in voting money should not expect to be put in the position of being the real managers of the railway. My understanding is that by circular ET-1, which is an order in council type of thing, the government in July of 1959 by executive decree deleted the trade of tinsmith from certain advantages of exemption with respect to the imposition of the 11 per cent sales tax. In consequence there has been a fair amount of havoc and consternation. I hope that the parliamentary secretary will indicate that this proposal in the resolution before us, as I hope is the case, is designed to bring tinsmiths back to their former status whereby they had for a long time enjoyed exemption from sales tax with respect to their work.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT
speechtext:
I think, Mr. Chairman, it could be said that this particular paragraph merely provides for the continuation of an existing exemption which has been welcomed on behalf of the industry by the Canadian warm air heating and air conditioning contractors association, who have extended to the Minister of Finance their warm and sincere thanks for this particular exemption. I would not wish the hon. gentleman to think that this restores in full the position

as it was prior to the particular direction of the Minister of National Revenue to which he referred, but it does in fact restore it in relation to ducts for warm air systems for the heating of buildings, and so on that basis has been warmly welcomed.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT
speechtext: I wonder if the parliamentary secretary could tell us why the change was made by the government, and what effect this has on the cost of small houses?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT
speechtext: I think, Mr. Chairman, the effect of this amendment on the cost of small houses is to restore it exactly to the position in which it was. I do not think there is any change whatever.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT
speechtext: Am I right in my understanding that because of this executive decree by order in council in July of 1959 the tinsmiths' work with respect to ducts for warm air systems became subject, in the meantime, to a tax of 11 per cent? The hon. member for Trinity would have more knowledge of this than I have, but the correspondence I have received appears to indicate that in the meantime there has probably been $30 or $40 extra added to the cost of homes. Would the parliamentary secretary know from the representations that have doubtless been made to him, as they have been made to me and others from the sheet metalworkers international association and the tinsmiths, as to whether or not that is a reasonable conclusion?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT
speechtext:
I would not be able to say, Mr. Chairman, as to whether that particular figure which the hon. gentleman states would be accurate. It is true that last July the Minister of National Revenue announced his intention of removing tinsmiths from the class of small manufacturers, except for those who met the general definition of a small manufacturer, which would be those whose actual volume was less than $3,000 worth of taxable goods sold exclusively to users.
In order to retain the exemption for one of the most important products of tinsmiths it is proposed by this amendment that ducts for warm air heating systems for heating buildings be the subject of specific exemption. They are listed in schedule 3 of the Excise Tax Act. This will cover as well stovepipes and all the ducts used in a heating system. I think the committee would be interested in the fact that under date of April 7 the general manager of the Canadian warm air heating and air conditioning contractors wrote the Minister of Finance, and I quote:
-may we convey our sincere thanks and appreciation for the recent exemption given to our industry re: ducts-warm air heating systems.
This exemption is further proof that our government is doing its share to decrease the cost of new house construction to the Canadian consumer.
Excise Tax Act
Your sympathetic understanding as to the many problems that would have been created by the enactment of circular ET-1 has been noted from coast to coast in Canada.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT
speechtext:
I am sure that this is an improvement upon the decision that was taken, as I say, by the executive by order in council a year ago, which was quite arbitrary and a great shock to the trade. But am I not right in thinking that there remains the substantial change, that is, the name of tinsmith is no longer to remain as a part of the regulations and not one of those trades named in section 3 of the regulations, subsection (b), describing a manufacturer? In consequence
I	imagine that a house builder, from the time of this edict last summer, who needed eaves-troughing or air conditioning or other tinsmith work in connection with the construction of a house, would have had to pay an
II	per cent tax which they did not have to pay until this administration came into office.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT
speechtext: As the hon. gentleman is well aware a change in the regulations does not change what has been the practice of not imposing a sales tax on sheet metalwork done on the construction site, whether it be for flashings or roof work or for whatever else it may be.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT
speechtext: May I draw the attention of the parliamentary secretary to the reference to $3,000 in the regulation? I take it that the amount of $3,000 is not set by this committee, but is set by the executive to whom parliament has given the power to decide upon the merits. I do not know when this $3,000 was set as the limit of the output of a small manufacturer.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT
speechtext: It is hallowed by tradition, I think.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT
speechtext:
I think, then, we should think about this hallowing, perhaps, and I wonder what consideration is being given to the fact that manufacturers' costs have increased substantially, I imagine, from the time this $3,000 limit was established in the regulations. If the executive has the power to set the $3,000 limit, it has the power to increase the limit. I wonder if consideration could be given to this, having regard to the increased cost of production of all things, even those things that are included here. It may have been something that the previous administration could have considered for many years, as I do not know how long this has been hallowed, but I think it deserves consideration because $3,000 no longer describes the output of a manufacturer. He could not live on the profit from a $3,000 output.

Excise Tax Act

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT
speechtext: I have no doubt the figure was before my hon. friend when he was in the role which I now occupy-

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT
speechtext: I do not recall it being before me.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT
speechtext: -as it has been before me from time to time. I can only assure my hon. friend these matters are under constant review.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT
speechtext:
I should like to add my voice to the objection raised by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River because I too have had representations from tinsmiths who have regretted the fact they are no longer eligible to be classed as manufacturers and to have their production exempted from sales tax.
However, I should like to raise another matter here, and that is the discrimination against wholesalers. This amendment refers to manufacturers, and while manufacturers are able to sell their wares to consumers, they are obligated to collect this sales tax only on the materials used in their manufacture if the product ends up in the hands of the wholesaler. He then has to pay this sales tax on the whole unit. If he resells he is under a severe handicap as opposed to the manufacturer who, in the case of this particular product, often has direct deals. I should like to move, therefore:
That the resolution be amended by eliminating therefrom the words, "but not including materials used in their manufacture."
This, I feel, would place the wholesaler on the same level as the manufacturer now is.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT
speechtext: Shall I put the amendment?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, perhaps before you leave the chair the house leader would indicate what is to be expected for tomorrow.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, for tomorrow there will be the third reading of Bill No. S-2, an act to amend the Canada-Netherlands Income Tax Agreement Act; then second reading of the bill with regard to the international development association, of which the resolution was passed today. Then I would like to carry on with the budget resolutions, but at four o'clock, due to the required absence of the Minister of Finance, if we are not finished with the budget resolutions I would like to adjourn that debate and commence with the estimates of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration and carry on with those estimates on Thursday, if necessary. That will be followed on Thursday by the estimates of the post office, and then for Friday we would commence with the estimates of the Department of Transport, followed by mines and technical surveys and fisheries, and fit in post office if that is not completed on the Thursday. It is a slight change in the order but the departments are the same which I named last week.

I wonder if the house leader will consider adhering to the statement he made earlier and start with the estimates of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration on Thursday morning? And if any estimates are taken tomorrow, could we take the Department of Transport estimates, because it would be much more convenient to us on this side to start with a new department on a new day.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: That is quite agreeable to me, if it suits the minister. Then transport estimates tomorrow at four o'clock.
